pages.title: How to use this volume
pages.html:
The revision companion

One integrated volume, designed to move between the original Diploma learning units, added clinical explanations and the published learning outcomes. Use it as a study guide and a reference during revision.

I The 14 Diploma units

Original content retained

The core that teaches the material. Anatomy, materials, assessment, removable and fixed prosthodontics, occlusion, implants, maintenance, governance and high-yield numbers.

II Integrated companion notes

Additional reading inserted by unit

Selected Fellowship material consolidated into the appropriate Diploma units. Extra clinical context explains decision-making, prevention, imaging, tooth wear, aesthetics and digital workflow.

III Syllabus and source maps

Learning-outcome alignment

The August 2026 Diploma learning-outcome domains guide the depth of revision. The integration and reference map on the next page shows where the additional material belongs.

A simple study cycle

1 READ

core unit

2 CONNECT

added notes

3 APPLY

case / SBA

4 REPAIR

weak LO

Read the core unit first. Follow immediately with its integrated notes, then test whether you can explain the diagnosis, first safe action, alternatives, consent, follow-up and referral. Revisit the associated learning-outcome code when an answer is weak.

Diploma scope at a glance

Applied knowledge 1.1–1.11 Basic biological sciences

Clinical judgement 2a.1–2a.21 Assessment and diagnosis

Clinical judgement 2b.1–2b.12 Treatment planning and management

Clinical judgement 2c.1–2c.27 Prosthodontic-specific planning

Good practice 3a.1–3a.12 Clinical governance

Good practice 3b.1–3b.5 Communication

Scope note. These are Level 2 / enhanced-skills outcomes, not the specialist Fellowship blueprint. Advanced specialist interventions are not presented as Diploma requirements; know when to refer. The original notebook describes 150 SBAs in 180 minutes, but the supplied learning outcomes independently specify only the written and SOE components. Confirm the current examination instructions.

pages.html:
DIPLOMA IN PROSTHODONTICS / VOLUME I

Edition 2 | Clinical update

Original 14 units retained; 32 new clinical decision pages inserted by unit

HOW TO USE THIS EDITION

Read the original unit first; then read its new clinical decision notes before attempting the matching topic in the 1,500-item Volume II bank. The source illustrations and author details are retained. The old pre-expansion question-number ranges printed in earlier editions are replaced here by topic-block letters A-N - not by a fabricated contiguous numerical sequence.

Updated Volume II topic crosswalk

UNIT 1 Applied anatomy A UNIT 2 Physiology/pathology B

UNIT 3 Dental materials C UNIT 4 Medical / pharmacology D

UNIT 5 Assessment / diagnosis E UNIT 6 RPD F

UNIT 7 Complete dentures G UNIT 8 Fixed prosthodontics H

UNIT 9 Occlusion / TMD I UNIT 10 Failing dentition / trauma J

UNIT 11 Implants / digital K UNIT 12 Complications L

UNIT 13 Governance M UNIT 14 Integrated cases N

INTERPRETATION AND LIMITATIONS

The Diploma examines an enhanced-skills / Level 2 clinician, not unrestricted specialist operative competence. The new notes bring selected previous membership-paper themes down to safe Diploma decision-making. Numerical examples are context dependent. New pages support clinical reasoning but are not official RCSEd materials and have not been independently examiner-calibrated.

Reference codes on new pages: LO, NH, RC, BSP, EFP, IM, IADT, SD, MC, BAD, M.

Full source names and clinical guidance locations are summarised in the final update note.

Author retained: Dr. Kam O Man, Owen November 2026 | Clinical update

pages.title: Unit 1: Applied anatomy
pages.html:
UNIT 1 Applied anatomy

IN ONE MINUTE

All four muscles of mastication are first-arch, supplied by V3 and fed by the maxillary artery; only the lateral pterygoid opens the mouth.

Elevators: masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid. Main retractor: posterior temporalis.

V3: anterior division motor except buccal; posterior division sensory except the nerve to mylohyoid.

Denture borders are set by muscles:

m odiolus, masseter, mylohyoid, and the coronoid process.

All four muscles of mastication develop from the first pharyngeal arch, are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigem inal nerve (V3), and receive blood from branches of the maxillary artery. The lateral pterygoid is the only one that opens the mouth.

mandible to the opposite side

EXAM TR A P S

The medial pterygoid nerve comes off the main trunk of V3; it also carries fibres through the otic ganglion to tensor veli palatini and tensor tym pani.

The masseter and medial pterygoid forma sling around the angle of the mandible.

Disc displacem ent and TM J clicking and locking are most associated with the lateral pterygoid (superior head attaches to the disc).

M asseteric hypertrophy is a sign of bruxism ; temporalis is the muscle most often palpably tender in tension-type

headache linked to TM D .

1.2 Mandibular nerve (V3) branches

Main trunk: nervus spinosus (m eningeal branch) and nerve to medial pterygoid.

Anterior division (m ainly m otor): m asseteric, deep temporal, nerve to lateral pterygoid, and the buccal (long buccal) nerve — the only sensory branch of the anterior division.

Posterior division (m ainly sensory): auriculotem poral (em braces the middle m eningeal artery; secretom otor to parotid), lingual (joined by chorda tym pani), inferior alveolar (gives the nerve to mylohyoid, motor to mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric; ends as mental and incisive nerves).

1.3 Maxillary artery

From the external carotid, behind the condylar neck.

PART POS ITIO N BRANCHES

1st (m andibular) Behind neck of condyle Deep auricular, anterior tympanic, middle m eningeal (through foram en spinosum ), accessory m eningeal, inferior alveolar

2nd (pterygoid) Related to lower head of lateral pterygoid

Deep temporal, pterygoid, m asseteric, buccal

3rd (pterygopalatine)

In pterygopalatine fossa Posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, descending (greater and lesser) palatine, artery of pterygoid canal, pharyngeal, sphenopalatine

Venous drainage of the muscles is to the pterygoid venous plexus, which communicates with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins — the route for intracranial spread of infection. Lymph from the muscles drains to deep cervical nodes.

1.4 Other muscles that move the mandible or shape dentures

Posterior belly of digastric Facial nerve (V II) Elevates hyoid

Mylohyoid Nerve to mylohyoid (V3) Floor of mouth; limits lingual flange of lower denture in the molar region

G eniohyoid C1 via hypoglossal nerve Depresses mandible, pulls hyoid forward

S tylohyoid Facial nerve Elevates and retracts hyoid

1.5 Tem porom andibular joint

Type: synovial, ginglym oarthrodial (hinge and gliding) joint; articular surfaces covered by fibrocartilage (not hyaline), reflecting its intram em branous origin.

Disc: biconcave and avascular centrally; posteriorly the bilam inar zone (retrodiscal tissue) is vascular and innervated — the source of pain in disc displacem ent.

Com partm ents: lower = rotation (first 20–25 mm of opening); upper = translation.

Ligam ents: lateral (tem porom andibular) ligam ent is the true stabiliser and limits posterior and inferior m ovem ent; sphenom andibular (from spine of sphenoid to lingula) and stylom andibular are accessory.

Nerve supply: auriculotem poral (m ain), m asseteric and deep temporal (H ilton's law ).

Blood: superficial temporal and maxillary arteries.

The post-dam lies between anterior and posterior vibrating lines; fovea palatini are a guide to its position.

The ham ular (pterygom axillary) notch marks the posterior limit of the tuberosity and the post-dam 's lateral extent; the pterygom andibular raphe runs from ham ulus to retrom olar region.

P arotid duct opens opposite the upper second molar; it can be compressed by an over-extended buccal flange.

pages.title: S01 | Clinical anatomy in decision-making
pages.html:
Source bridge · F Pros Chapter 1

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 1.1, 1.5, 1.11 · 2a.5–2a.6

CORE PRINCIPLE

Translate anatomy into risk, denture extension and examination findings—not an isolated list of muscle names.

01 Functional anatomy at the chairside

Map the muscles and frena to the denture borders: lip and cheek muscles shape the polished surface; the mylohyoid, retromylohyoid area and tongue control lower lingual extension. An apparently retentive denture may still be unstable if its contours conflict with muscle movement.

02 Structures that alter the plan

In an atrophic mandible, consider the proximity of the mental nerve to the denture-bearing surface. In the maxilla, examine palatal form, tuberosities and soft-palate movement before deciding the posterior palatal seal or a palatal connector.

03 Risk and referral

Anatomical complexity becomes clinically relevant when it changes radiographic selection, impression design or safety. Spreading infection with airway concern, complex soft-tissue pathology or unexplained neuropathy requires escalation; detailed surgery is outside this Diploma supplement.

04 One-best-answer cue

A short mandibular lingual flange may lose the seal; excessive extension can dislodge the denture during tongue action. Diagnose the functional border before changing the occlusion or adding adhesive.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Level 2: recognition, examination, prosthesis design and timely referral. No specialist anatomical surgery is implied.

Source material: F Pros pp. 8–10 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 1: Functional anatomy that changes the denture
pages.html:
Functional anatomy that changes the denture

APPLIED ANATOMY

CORE PRINCIPLE

Retention at rest does not prove stability during speech, mastication or tongue movement. Decide which border or polished surface is displaced during a functional test before changing the occlusion.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Distobuccal lower flange lifts on forceful closureMasseter contracts against an excessive flangeReassess the masseteric notch during functional border moulding
Lingual lower flange rises on swallowingMylohyoid and tongue move the floor of mouthDifferentiate overextension from inadequate retromylohyoid form
Upper denture dislodges on wide openingCoronoid movement can engage a thick distobuccal flangeCheck tuberosity undercuts, flange bulk and functional clearance
Sore at incisive papilla or high mental foramenNeurovascular structures lie under thin, resorbed tissuesRelieve pressure and investigate unexplained persistent sensory change

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The decisive distinction is movement-related displacement versus inadequate static adaptation. A new denture may pass a finger-pull test yet dislodge whenever the patient smiles. Observe the causal movement and use pressure indicating paste before removing acrylic.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A lower denture is stable at rest but rises during protrusion of the tongue. Border extension and polished-surface form are the first checks; increasing vertical dimension or providing an adhesive is less defensible.

EXAM TRAP

Never attribute unilateral persistent lower-lip paraesthesia to denture pressure without investigation.

pages.title: Unit 2: Physiology and pathology
pages.html:
UNIT 2 Physiology and pathology

IN ONE MINUTE

Frequency of sugar and acid, not the total amount, drives caries and erosion; saliva both retains dentures and protects teeth.

Critical pH : enamel 5.5, root 6.2–6.7, fluorapatite 4.5.

After tooth loss the maxilla resorbs centripetally, the mandible centrifugally, and the anterior mandible about four

times faster.

A n ulcer that persists 3 weeks after

removing the cause is an urgent referral; erythroplakia carries the highest

malignant risk.

After tooth loss the residual ridge resorbs fastest in the first 6–12 months and continues for life; the anterior mandible loses

about four times as much height as the anterior maxilla in the longterm (Tallgren).

2.1 Saliva

V olum e: about 0.5–1.5 L/day. U nstim ulated flow about 0.3–0.4 m L/m in. H yposalivation = unstim ulated below 0.1 m L/m in or

stimulated below about 0.5–0.7 m L/m in.

Functions: lubrication, buffering (bicarbonate main buffer in stimulated saliva), rem ineralisation, antim icrobial (lysozym e, lactoferrin, IgA , histatins), taste, bolus formation, denture retention.

Denture retention depends on a thin film of saliva: adhesion (saliva to mucosa and denture), cohesion (w ithin saliva), interfacial surface tension, viscosity, and atmospheric pressure via the border (peripheral) seal. Thin watery saliva gives better retention than thick ropy saliva.

Common causes of dry mouth: drugs (antidepressants, antihistam ines, antim uscarinics, diuretics, antipsychotics), S jögren's syndrom e, head and neck radiotherapy, poorly controlled diabetes, dehydration, anxiety, mouth breathing.

M anagem ent: treat cause, sugar-free stimulants, saliva substitutes (m ucin- or carboxym ethylcellulose-based; avoid acidic substitutes in dentate patients), pilocarpine (contraindicated in asthm a, glaucom a), high-fluoride toothpaste.

2.2 Mastication and neurom uscular control

Periodontal m echanoreceptors give fine tactile and load feedback; they are lost in the edentulous patient, so complete denture wearers depend on mucosal and TM J receptors. Implants give "osseoperception", less sensitive than a natural tooth.

Complete denture wearers achieve roughly one-fifth to one-sixth of the bite force and m asticatory efficiency of dentate people.

Shortened dental arch (K äyser): an arch of prem olars and anterior teeth (about 3–5 occlusal units) usually gives adequate function in older adults; replacing missing m olars with a free-end RPD often adds little.

WHO goal: retention of at least 20 functional teeth throughout life.

Ability to adapt to new dentures falls with age, neurom uscular disease (P arkinson's), dementia and stroke: favour copy (replica) techniques.

2.3 Consequences of tooth loss

Pattern: maxilla resorbs upwards and inw ards (centripetal), making the upper arch smaller; mandible resorbs dow nw ards and outwards (centrifugal), making it wider. Result: an apparent Class III relationship and posterior crossbite in long-term edentulous patients.

Local factors: drifting, tilting and over-eruption of opposing teeth (reducing interocclusal space), loss of occlusal vertical dimension, loss of lip and cheek support.

2.4 C aries

Critical pH : enamel (hydroxyapatite) about 5.5; root dentine and cem entum about 6.2–6.7; fluorapatite about 4.5.

Stephan curve: pH falls within minutes of sugar intake and recovers in 30–60 minutes; frequency of intake matters more than quantity.

Microbiology: Streptococcus m utans (initiation; acidogenic, aciduric, extracellular polysaccharides), Lactobacillus (progression in cavitated lesions), A ctinom yces (root caries). Ecological plaque hypothesis: environm ental change (frequent sugar, low saliva) selects for acid-producing species.

E nam el lesion zones (deep to surface): translucent zone, dark zone, body of lesion (largest dem ineralisation), surface zone (relatively intact).

Dentine lesion zones: infected (soft, bacteria-laden, rem ove) and affected (dem ineralised, rem ineralisable, can be left in

selective rem oval).

Delivering Better Oral Health (2021): adults 1450 ppm F toothpaste, spit don't rinse; high-risk adults 5000 ppm (16 and over) or 2800 ppm (10 and over); fluoride varnish 22,600 ppm at least twice yearly for those at higher risk.

Root caries risk rises with recession, hyposalivation, partial dentures (plaque retention around clasps and saddles), poor dexterity, and frequent sugar.

pages.title: S02 | Prevention as part of prosthodontic care
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 4 → Diploma Unit 2

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 1.4, 1.8 · 2b.3–2b.5 · 2c.1

CORE PRINCIPLE

Every definitive restoration or prosthesis depends on disease control and realistic maintenance.

01 High-yield preventive advice

The source F Pros notes cite Delivering Better Oral Health v4: brush twice daily with 1,350–1,500 ppm fluoride toothpaste, then spit without rinsing. Higher-fluoride products and varnish are selected by caries risk, age, medical history and the current prescribing guidance.

02 A workable sequence

Control sugar and acid frequency, tobacco use, plaque accumulation and active periodontal disease before definitive treatment. The F Pros notes summarise periodontal care as oral hygiene/risk-factor control → subgingival instrumentation → surgery where necessary → supportive periodontal care.

03 Denture-specific prevention

Take dentures out overnight and clean them with non-abrasive products. Sodium hypochlorite can damage cobalt-chromium; avoid it for metal frameworks. Manage denture stomatitis by addressing fit and hygiene as well as candidal infection.

04 Patient factors change designs

Xerostomia can impair retention and increase caries and candidosis. When cleaning or attendance will be unreliable, favour hygienic, maintainable designs rather than elaborate fixed work that the patient cannot support.

05 SBA traps

Miconazole interacts with warfarin; check current prescribing advice. Deep caries may favour selective caries removal rather than complete removal over the pulp. Do not assume every missing tooth needs replacement.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Prescribing and recall figures are source-derived teaching points; use current local guidelines for clinical care.

Source material: F Pros pp. 16–17 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 2: Oral candidosis and inhaler-related lesions
pages.html:
Oral candidosis and inhaler-related lesions

PHYSIOLOGY AND PATHOLOGY

CORE PRINCIPLE

The first choice depends on the lesion, host risk and drug interaction - not simply the presence of an inhaler.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Removable white plaques; erythematous basePseudomembranous candidosis Check cause, denture hygiene, inhaler technique and need for antifungal
Diffuse erythema under upper dentureErythematous denture-associated candidosisCorrect fit, night wear and cleaning before repeated drug courses
Nodular papillary palatal surfaceInflammatory papillary hyperplasiaAssess trauma and exclude another lesion; refer when indicated
Asthma patient on inhaled steroid, not just salbutamolLocal corticosteroid deposition raises oral candidosis riskRinse/gargle and spit after steroid; consider spacer; treat active infection if needed

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Salbutamol is a short-acting beta-agonist, not an inhaled corticosteroid. Ask whether the patient also uses beclometasone, budesonide or fluticasone. For a mild steroid-associated problem, address inhaler technique and local measures. Confirm candidosis before prescribing repeated antifungals; consider sampling when atypical or recurrent.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

Patient A uses salbutamol alone with non-wipeable leukoplakia: do not label this candidosis. Patient B uses inhaled budesonide with wipeable plaques and soreness: correct inhaler technique, identify predisposing factors and treat confirmed infection.

EXAM TRAP

Miconazole can potentiate warfarin; oral agents require a medication interaction check.

pages.html:
Burning mouth, altered taste and oral paraesthesia

PHYSIOLOGY AND PATHOLOGY

CORE PRINCIPLE

A symptom such as burning or pins-and-needles is a presentation, not automatically a diagnosis of burning mouth syndrome.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Visible erythema, depapillation or plaquesCandidosis, contact irritation or nutritional deficiencyExamine mucosa, review dentures/drugs; investigate as indicated
Bilateral daily burning with clinically normal mucosaPossible primary burning mouth disorder after exclusionCharacterise distribution, duration, xerostomia and neuropathic features
Unilateral numbness or progressive sensory lossLocal nerve injury, compression or serious pathologyDocument neurosensory deficit and arrange urgent assessment
Intermittent shooting, triggerable facial painNeuralgia or another neuropathic conditionAvoid irreversible dental treatment without clear odontogenic evidence

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Investigations should follow findings: full blood count, ferritin/iron, B12, folate or glycaemic assessment when appropriate; salivary status, medications and candidal risk may explain symptoms. Trauma, dental local anaesthesia and surgery can produce focal sensory deficits; red flags include evolving numbness and a persistent ulcer or mass.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A woman with bilateral burning, normal mucosa and normal targeted tests differs fundamentally from an older patient with new unilateral tongue numbness. The first warrants a working neuropathic diagnosis and appropriate referral; the second needs timely investigation.

EXAM TRAP

Do not offer endodontics, occlusal adjustment or denture remakes as empirical treatment for unexplained neuropathic pain.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 2: Developmental enamel and dentine disorders
pages.html:
Developmental enamel and dentine disorders

PHYSIOLOGY AND PATHOLOGY

CORE PRINCIPLE

Use distribution, family history, radiographic features and the pattern of tissue weakness to separate defects in enamel quantity, mineralisation and dentine.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Thin enamel with generally normal radiodensityHypoplastic amelogenesis imperfecta (AI)Adhesive/restorative planning depends on the remaining enamel
Normal thickness but soft or poorly mineralised enamelHypomaturation/hypocalcified AI Early wear, sensitivity and bonding uncertainty; consider protection
Opalescent teeth, bulbous crowns, cervical narrowingDentinogenesis imperfecta (DI) Radiographs may show early pulp obliteration; protect weak dentine
Symmetric diffuse opacities; exposure historyDental fluorosis versus localised hypoplasiaAssess timing/distribution before selecting microabrasion or resin infiltration

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

AI is often generalised and familial, while a single affected tooth suggests a local developmental or traumatic insult. DI may be associated with osteogenesis imperfecta; an absence of family history does not rule it out. Severity and stage of development direct preventive, transitional and definitive treatment.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A teenager with soft, rapidly wearing teeth in both arches needs protective occlusal planning and longitudinal care, not automatic full crowns on every tooth. In a patient with well-demarcated white spots confined to one region, investigate local aetiology before diagnosing familial AI.

EXAM TRAP

Do not confuse enamel hypoplasia (less enamel formed) with hypomineralisation (poorer enamel quality).

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 2: Erosive lichen planus, pemphigoid and pemphigus
pages.html:
Erosive lichen planus, pemphigoid and pemphigus

PHYSIOLOGY AND PATHOLOGY

CORE PRINCIPLE

Desquamative gingivitis and painful oral erosions have several causes. The urgency of referral depends on malignancy risk, ocular/airway involvement and systemic disease - not a fixed ranking of review intervals.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Bilateral reticular striae; sometimes erosionsOral lichen planus may have symptomatic erosive diseaseAssess changes, triggers and need for biopsy/specialist review
Persistent painful erosive lesion or red-white patchPotential dysplasia or an alternative diagnosisRisk-based review and biopsy for atypical/persistent change
Desquamative gingivitis; ocular irritation or scarringMucous membrane pemphigoid is a key differentialUrgent oral medicine and ophthalmology assessment
Widespread fragile bullae, extensive erosionsPemphigus vulgaris can cause serious mucocutaneous diseasePrompt specialist assessment and systemic coordination

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

A clinical appearance alone cannot reliably distinguish immunobullous disorders. Specialist biopsy for routine histology and perilesional direct immunofluorescence may be required. Oral lichen planus needs long-term symptom and lesion surveillance; mucous membrane pemphigoid can cause irreversible ocular scarring, while pemphigus may require systemic immunosuppression.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A patient with reticular striae and stable small oral erosions is not managed identically to one with sloughing gingiva, painful red eyes and progressive scarring. The latter needs urgent assessment for pemphigoid with ocular involvement.

EXAM TRAP

Do not rank all three diseases by a single fixed recall frequency: activity, systemic involvement and suspicious changes determine urgency.

More water → weaker, lower expansion, slower set. More spatulation → faster set, more expansion.

Accelerators: potassium sulphate, gypsum seed (slurry), sodium chloride (low concentration). R etarders: borax, citrates,

H ygroscopic expansion occurs if the setting mass is immersed in water. Dry strength is about twice wet strength.

3.4 Waxes and investm ents

Inlay wax has high therm al expansion and releases stresses (distortion) if left before investing: invest promptly.

Gypsum -bonded investm ent: gold alloys only; calcium sulphate breaks down above about 700°C releasing sulphur dioxide.

P hosphate-bonded investm ent: m etal–ceram ic and base-m etal (Co-Cr, N i-C r) alloys; higher temperature.

Investm ent expansion (setting, hygroscopic, therm al) compensates for alloy casting shrinkage (gold about 1.4% ; Co-Cr about 2.3% ).

Dough stages: sandy → stringy (sticky) → dough (pack now ) → rubbery → stiff.

P olym erisation shrinkage: m onom er alone about 21% by volum e; dough about 7% volum e, about 0.5% linear. Water uptake partly compensates.

Gaseous porosity: heating too fast som onom er boils (100.3°C ) → bubbles in the thickest section. Contraction porosity: too little dough or pressure → voids throughout and at the surface. Granular porosity: m onom er evaporation from dough left uncovered.

Residual m onom er: heat-cured about 0.2–0.5% ; self-cured (chem ically activated, am ine) about 2–5% — irritant and allergenic; self-cured is weaker and discolours (am ine oxidation) but distorts less.

pages.title: S03 | Choosing a restorative material
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 11 → Diploma Unit 3

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 1.9 · 2c.6, 2c.13–2c.14

CORE PRINCIPLE

Most materials questions are clinical-choice problems: match properties, preparation, substrate and maintenance.

01 Bonding must match the substrate

Silica-based glass ceramics such as lithium disilicate require a suitable hydrofluoric-acid/silane-based protocol according to manufacturer directions. Zirconia is not etched in the same way; the F Pros source emphasises airborne-particle abrasion and MDP chemistry.

02 Preparations and restorability

A short, over-tapered crown preparation cannot be repaired by simply using more cement. Consider height, resistance form and an adhesive or auxiliary feature. A post retains a core; it does not strengthen a root-filled tooth.

03 What failures reveal

Layered ceramics are more vulnerable to chipping in some parafunctional settings; monolithic options may reduce the veneer fracture mode. Soft-tissue inflammation may indicate an overcontoured or deep subgingival margin rather than a defective ceramic itself.

04 Cost-benefit and consent

Compare repairability, retrievability, opposing-tooth wear, tooth reduction, aesthetics, laboratory workflow and replacement cost. Patient preference matters only after the clinical contraindications and maintenance requirements are explained.

05 Exam comparison

E-modulus tells you about stiffness, not toughness. Do not confuse flexural strength with wear behaviour, or high strength with a good bond. Treat the manufacturer-specific protocols as decisive.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Select treatment within competence. Do not convert laboratory handling principles into unsupervised specialist procedures.

Source material: F Pros pp. 33–34; 18–20 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 3: PMMA processing: timing, heat and residual monomer
pages.html:
PMMA processing: timing, heat and residual monomer

DENTAL MATERIALS SCIENCE

CORE PRINCIPLE

An acrylic denture that deforms, tastes of monomer or becomes porous may have distinct processing errors. Identify which stage created the defect.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Shortened heat cure or low conversionMore residual methyl methacrylate and lower conversionAssess biocompatibility, strength, curing cycle and need for remake
Excessive temperature reached in thick acrylicMonomer boiling and internal gaseous porosityCheck heating schedule and bulk; do not assume contamination
Packing before dough stage or with inadequate materialDimensional instability, voids or surface defectsReview packing stage and flask closure pressure
Large cold-cure repair in a stressed baseHigher residual monomer and variable interface strengthUse an appropriate repair protocol; manage underlying flexion

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Heat-cured PMMA is generally preferred for definitive bases where appropriate processing can limit residual monomer and optimise properties. Autopolymerising PMMA is convenient for repairs but may be less completely converted. Polymerisation shrinkage, cooling contraction and water sorption affect dimensional accuracy; they are not interchangeable explanations.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A thick upper denture has internal spherical voids after accelerated heating: think gaseous porosity. An otherwise intact repair smells of residual monomer and irritates the mucosa: examine cure and material selection instead.

EXAM TRAP

Do not memorise one curing time as universal; cycles differ between materials and manufacturers.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 3: PMMA porosity: distinguish four mechanisms
pages.html:
PMMA porosity: distinguish four mechanisms

DENTAL MATERIALS SCIENCE

CORE PRINCIPLE

The location and appearance of voids often reveal the laboratory fault better than a generic label of "poor processing".

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Round pores centred in thick palateBoiling of monomer when exotherm/temperature too highControl heating rate and max temperature for the resin
Irregular voids throughout dough or along surfacesInsufficient dough, packing pressure or flask closureCorrect material amount, packing and trial closure
Fine granular porosity near surfaceMonomer lost as dough left exposed or dry mixingLimit exposure; follow powder-liquid ratio and packing window
Porosity localised near a repair junctionContamination, inadequate adaptation or repair techniqueAssess interface preparation, wetting and polymerisation

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

A material may be hard yet still weak if a void acts as a stress concentrator. Investigate the site of the pores, processing record and cross-sectional bulk. Defect localisation often differentiates heat-related from packing-related problems.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

Two identical upper dentures crack: one has voids in the thick palatal part following rapid heating; the other has internal gaps and flash after inadequate trial packing. The prevention methods differ despite the shared word "porosity".

EXAM TRAP

Porosity is a structural defect; adding more chairside acrylic to the surface may disguise it without restoring strength.

pages.html:
Denture crack propagation, fatigue and repairs

DENTAL MATERIALS SCIENCE

CORE PRINCIPLE

Fracture analysis should work backwards from crack origin, load direction and clinical fit. Replacing the acrylic alone is not a diagnosis.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Repeated midline upper denture fracture in functionCyclic tensile stress, flexure and a stress raiserCheck occlusion, base thickness, high vault/torus and support
Sudden irregular fracture after dropping dentureImpact failure Consider impact-resistant material and patient handling
Crack originating at frenum notch or sharp angleLocal stress concentration Round internal angles and correct design geometry
Refracture precisely at old cold-cure junctionWeaker repair zone plus persisting flexionAddress cause, reprocess/remake or reinforce appropriately

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Fatigue crack growth can occur below a material's single-load fracture strength. A scratch, porosity, unsupported free end or sharp frenum notch raises local tensile stress. A cold-cure addition changes residual monomer and bond characteristics but does not remove abnormal loading.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

After a second repaired fracture the base continues to flex against a firm palatal torus and heavy anterior contacts. A new high-impact material may help; the decisive intervention is to correct support, relief and occlusal load rather than repeatedly adding autopolymerising resin.

EXAM TRAP

Excess reinforcement can shift stress to another thin section; design and support must be reviewed together.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 3: Cast, wrought and polymer clasps: why undercuts differ
pages.html:
Cast, wrought and polymer clasps: why undercuts differ

DENTAL MATERIALS SCIENCE

CORE PRINCIPLE

Undercut depth cannot be chosen by material name alone. Elastic deflection also depends on clasp length, taper, cross-section and path of insertion.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Typical cast Co-Cr circumferential claspStiff alloy with limited allowable deflectionOften about 0.25 mm undercut; assess design and tooth mobility
Cast gold clasp with appropriate geometryLower modulus and greater ductility than Co-CrAround 0.5 mm may be used in suitable designs
Wrought wire clasp Longer flexible arm and favourable fatigue responseDeeper engagement may be feasible, often around 0.5 mm
Flexible polyamide or other polymer claspMaterial- and thickness-dependent deflectionDo not automatically equate 0.75 mm with any polymer clasp

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The 0.25/0.5/0.75 mm gauges identify available retentive undercuts; they do not prescribe a material without considering retention, abutment prognosis and oral anatomy. Rigid connectors provide support and bracing, while the terminal retentive arm must flex within its elastic range.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A short, thick Co-Cr arm placed into a 0.5 mm undercut on a mobile canine risks excessive force. A longer appropriately designed wrought arm might be considered, but the abutment condition and surveyed path still govern selection.

EXAM TRAP

Aesthetic polymer clasps are not equivalent to a properly supported, adjustable Co-Cr framework.

pages.html:
Ceramics, impression errors and Co-Cr casting faults

DENTAL MATERIALS SCIENCE

CORE PRINCIPLE

Different materials fail through different stages: loss of impression accuracy, casting distortion, inadequate surface treatment or unsuitable crown geometry.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
PVS wash fails to set near retraction cordSulphur/chemical contamination may inhibit addition siliconeCheck latex and haemostatic product compatibility
Polyether impression deformed on removalHigh stiffness, especially in deep undercutsEvaluate material selection, block-out and removal path
Metal-ceramic crown chips on coolingThermal-expansion mismatch or unsupported porcelainInvestigate coping support and alloy-ceramic compatibility
Co-Cr framework has short cast clasp or misfitPattern distortion, inadequate casting or finishing errorTrace defect to survey, wax-up, sprue, investment, casting and fitting

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

For a laboratory failure, locate the stage: master cast accuracy, surveyed design, refractory cast, wax pattern, spruing and investment, burnout/casting, finishing and try-in. A poor intraoral fit may also originate from distorted impressions or a flexible tray - not necessarily the casting machine.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

When several Co-Cr frameworks from one case fit the same inaccurate master cast but not the mouth, repeating the casting alone is unlikely to help. Confirm impression and cast accuracy first.

EXAM TRAP

Clinical fit, not a visually polished surface, is the final acceptance criterion.

UNIT 4 P harm acology, pain control, emergencies and the medically compromised patient

N um ber card 4

IN ONE MINUTE

Know the doses, never stop antiplatelets, and adjust DOAC s only for higher-risk procedures.

Adrenaline 500 µg IM ; G TN 400 µg; aspirin 300 mg; glucagon 1 mg IM .

W arfarin: treat if the IN R is under 4, checked within 24 hours.

MRONJ: in higher-risk patients retain roots rather than extract; no routine drug holiday.

In SBA son the medically compromised patient, the right answer usually keeps the drug going (antiplatelets, most

anticoagulants, antiresorptives), uses local measures, and changes how the prosthesis is planned rather than refusing care.

Doses below are adult and follow UK guidance (B N F, SDCEP , Resuscitation Council UK ); always check the current versions.

4.1 Local anaesthetics

AGENT PRESEN TA TIO N (UKCAR TR ID G E ) PO IN TS TO REMEMBER

Lidocaine 2% with 1:80,000 adrenaline (2.2 m L = 44 m g)

A m ide; reference agent; max dose with adrenaline commonly quoted 4.4 m g/kg in

dental texts (B N F upper limit higher)

1:200,000 adrenaline

A m ide with an ester side chain: rapid plasm a esterase metabolism , short half-life; good bone diffusion for infiltration; max about 7 m g/kg

P rilocaine 3% with felypressin 0.03

IU /m L

Use when adrenaline is a concern; felypressin has oxytocic action (avoid in late

pregnancy); high doses cause m ethaem oglobinaem ia

M epivacaine 3% plain Short duration; no vasoconstrictor

Toxicity: C N S first (perioral tingling, tinnitus, drowsiness, convulsions), then cardiovascular depression.

Adrenaline interactions: non-selective beta-blockers (hypertension with reflex bradycardia), tricyclic antidepressants, cocaine; limit dose in significant cardiac disease.

Failed inferior alveolar block causes: accessory innervation (mylohyoid nerve, cervical plexus), bifid canal, infection (low tissue pH reduces non-ionised fraction), anxiety, poor technique. Remedies: Gow -G ates or A kinosi block, articaine buccal infiltration, intraligam entary.

4.2 Sedation (U KIA C S D 2020 standards)

Inhalation sedation: nitrous oxide in oxygen titrated; machines deliver at least 30% oxygen (m axim um 70% N ₂O ); fail-safe and

scavenging required. Relative contraindications: first trimester pregnancy, nasal obstruction, severe COPD , recent middle ear

or eye surgery with gas, vitam in B 12 deficiency.

IV sedation: m idazolam titrated; antagonist flum azenil. Escort for 24 hours (adults treated with IV ), no driving or operating

machinery until next day. C ontraindications: pregnancy, severe COPD , severe liver disease, m yasthenia gravis, allergy.

Monitoring: pulse oxim etry and blood pressure for IV ; clinical monitoring for inhalation.

Primary care is generally for ASAI–II patients; A SA III+ to secondary care.

4.6 A ntiresorptive and antiangiogenic drugs (MRONJ)

Definition: exposed bone, or bone that can be probed through a fistula, in the m axillofacial region for more than 8 weeks, in a patient with a history of antiresorptive or antiangiogenic therapy and no history of radiotherapy to the jaws or obvious

metastatic disease.

Drugs: bisphosphonates (alendronic acid, risedronate oral; zoledronic acid, ibandronic acid IV ), denosum ab (RANKL antibody — effect wears off in months, unlike bisphosphonates which persist in bone for years), antiangiogenics (bevacizum ab, sunitinib).

Higher risk: cancer patients on high-dose IV bisphosphonate or denosum ab; osteoporosis patients on oral bisphosphonates over 5 years or with concurrent system ic glucocorticoids.

P rosthodontic implications: get the mouth healthy before starting treatm ent; w ell-fitting, w ell-extended dentures with relief over bony prominences; avoid traum atic flanges; prefer root retention (decoronate, overdenture abutm ents, endodontics) to

extraction; implants only after careful risk assessm ent and consent. SDCEP does not recom mend drug holidays for routine dentistry.

4.7 Head and neck radiotherapy

Effects: xerostom ia (perm anent if parotids in field), radiation caries (cervical, ram pant), m ucositis, trism us (fibrosis of muscles of m astication), candidosis, osteoradionecrosis (m andible farm ore than maxilla; risk lifelong, dose-dependent above about 50–

60 G y).

Before radiotherapy: dental assessm ent; extract teeth of poor prognosis with time to heal (ideally 10–14 days or more before starting).

After: 5000 ppm fluoride toothpaste, fluoride gel in custom trays, saliva substitutes, trism us exercises; dentures carefully adjusted with soft lining where mucosa is fragile; avoid extractions in the field if possible.

Implants in irradiated bone have higher failure rates; these patients and m axillofacial (obturator) prostheses are Level 3.

4.8 Diabetes

Diagnosis: H bA 1c of 48 mm ol/m ol (6.5% ) or above; prediabetes 42–47 mm ol/m ol.

Tw o-w ay relationship with periodontitis; also candidosis, xerostom ia, poor healing, burning mouth, higher implant complications when poorly controlled.

The Level 2 curriculum expects the dentist to identify at-risk patients and refer to the GM Por diabetic services for H bA 1c

testing, per MC N policy.

Book morning appointm ents after a normal meal; have oral glucose available.

pages.title: S04 | Medical risk and safe treatment sequencing
pages.html:
F Pros Chapters 1 and 4 → Diploma Unit 4

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 1.3, 1.7 · 2a.3, 2a.13–2a.14 · 2b.11–2b.12

CORE PRINCIPLE

The single best answer is often to recognise the modifier and adapt or defer care safely.

01 Assess the patient, not only the tooth

Record medical problems, allergies, anticoagulants, antiresorptives, immunosuppressants, glycaemic control, xerostomia and anxiety. Ask how each could affect treatment or healing rather than memorising a drug list.

02 Planning under uncertainty

When the patient has unstable disease or risk factors, stabilise oral disease, review medical information and decide whether liaison or referral is needed before elective definitive prosthodontics. Choose minimally invasive interventions when appropriate.

03 Communicate material risk

Include expected benefit, alternatives (including no treatment), maintenance costs, medical risk and any material clinical uncertainty in shared decision-making. Document the decision and any specialist advice.

04 Two traps

Uncontrolled periodontal disease is not a suitable foundation for new definitive bridgework. A patient on anticoagulants should not be instructed to stop medication simply because surgery is being considered; follow the relevant procedure-specific prescribing guidance.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Use the Diploma Unit 4 medication tables and up-to-date BNF/SDCEP/local emergency protocols for exact doses.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 4: Smoking, diabetes and medicines: risk is a modifier
pages.html:
Smoking, diabetes and medicines: risk is a modifier

MEDICAL RISK AND EMERGENCIES

CORE PRINCIPLE

Risk factors alter disease susceptibility, wound healing and treatment predictability; they do not replace site-specific diagnosis or justify blanket refusal of care.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Smoker with low visible bleeding but deep pocketsNicotine-related vascular effects can mask inflammationUse attachment, probing, radiographic bone loss and risk history
Poorly controlled diabetes before periodontal therapyHigher inflammatory burden and poorer responseLiaise on glycaemic control; stabilise disease and review
Previous periodontitis considering implantsElevated peri-implant disease susceptibilityAssess stability, hygiene, maintenance commitment and anatomy
Antiresorptive therapy or anticoagulantsProcedure-related risks and drug interactions varyIndividualise with current guidance; do not stop medication ad hoc

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Smoking and diabetes contribute to periodontal grade and prognosis. Successful periodontal treatment and supportive maintenance can improve outcomes, but uncontrolled systemic risk may require additional assessment and staged treatment. Dental prescribing must check interactions, especially antifungals and warfarin.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

Two patients have the same 6 mm pocket: one with controlled diabetes and good maintenance, the other a heavy smoker with rapid bone loss. Identical pocket depth does not imply identical progression risk or recall plan.

EXAM TRAP

No universal HbA1c or smoking threshold is sufficient on its own to determine every dental procedure.

UNIT 5 A ssessm ent, diagnosis, imaging and classifications

IN ONE MINUTE

Classify, stage and grade by the rules, then justify every radiograph.

Kennedy after planned extractions, with A pplegate's rules.

Classification questions are reliable marks: learn the exact definitions below , especially Kennedy with A pplegate's rules,

5.1 History and examination essentials

History: presenting complaint in the patient's words; expectations (aesthetic, functional); dental and denture history (age and number of previous dentures, what was good or bad about each); medical, drug, social (sm oking, alcohol, diet, occupation, motivation, dexterity) and family history.

E xtra-oral: facial sym m etry, lip support, lower face height, TM J (clicks, crepitus, deviation, opening), muscles of mastication, lymph nodes, smile line (high smile line shows more than 3 mm of gingiva — aesthetic risk).

Intra-oral: soft tissues and cancer screen; periodontal status (B P E , then full charting where codes 3 or 4); teeth and

restorations; edentulous ridges (height, width, shape, flabby tissue, undercuts, tori); saliva; occlusion (R C P , IC P , slide,

guidance, interferences, interocclusal space, O V D , freew ay space).

Existing dentures: retention, stability, support, extension, O V D , occlusion, aesthetics, hygiene, wear.

H ouse's classification of the edentulous patient's attitude: philosophical (best prognosis), exacting, indifferent, hysterical (sceptical).

5.2 Kennedy classification and A pplegate's rules

C LASS DESCR IP TIO N

Sensibility: cold (tetrafluoroethane or ethyl chloride on a pledget; more reliable than heat), electric pulp test (assesses nerve response, not blood supply; false negatives after traum a, in immature, calcified or older teeth; false positives with anxiety or liquefactive necrosis). Percussion and palpation, mobility, bite tests (Tooth S looth for cracked tooth), transillum ination.

Mounted study casts on a sem i-adjustable articulator with facebow and an R C P record: assess interocclusal space, plan w ax-

up, survey for RPD design.

Diagnostic w ax-up and m ock-up: test aesthetics, O V D , and communicate with the patient and laboratory.

Blood tests: FB C (low MC V suggests iron deficiency; high MC V suggests B 12 or folate deficiency), ferritin, B 12, folate; H bA 1c;

IN R for w arfarin.

5.9 Prognosis and restorability

Tooth prognosis depends on periodontal support, restorability (sound coronal dentine for a ferrule, caries extent), endodontic status, strategic value, and the patient's risk factors.

R estorability checklist: at least 1.5–2 mm ferrule possible without crown lengthening that would compromise the root; no subgingival caries extending into the root beyond reach; crow n–root ratio acceptable; no vertical root fracture; tooth is strategically useful.

Endodontic entry criteria in the N H S standard: teeth must be restorable with sound coronal tissue above the crest (about 2

mm high and 1 mm wide, or over 30% of the original crown volum e).

pages.title: S05 | Assessment and imaging: a decision pathway
pages.html:
F Pros Chapters 1–2 → Diploma Unit 5

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2a.1–2a.21 · 2b.6

CORE PRINCIPLE

Select investigations only when their results may change the diagnosis, prognosis or plan.

01 History → examination → hypothesis

Start with the patient’s concern, medical and dental history, risk factors and expectations. Examine soft tissue, hard tissue, periodontal support, denture-bearing tissues, tooth wear, function and occlusion. Generate a differential diagnosis before ordering further tests.

02 Choose the minimum useful imaging

Bitewings help with proximal caries and crestal bone; periapicals with periapical or root pathology; panoramic imaging for overview; CBCT only for an appropriate three-dimensional question that cannot be answered by lower-dose methods.

03 Interpret results together

A normal sensibility response does not prove vascular vitality, and radiographs have limitations. Periodontal attachment levels and clinical probing complement imaging. Read tests in the context of the history and other findings.

04 Record the implication

State whether a radiographic finding changes restorability, root configuration, bone support, anatomical safety or the feasible replacement options. Uncertain findings may require review, repeat tests or referral.

05 SBA traps

Do not select CBCT as routine screening; justify the field of view and radiation exposure. A normal radiograph does not overrule a concerning clinical examination or suspicious mucosal lesion.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

The F Pros imaging chapter informs Diploma investigation decisions, not specialist-level CBCT reporting.

pages.title: S06 | Treatment strategies and consent
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 3 → Diploma Unit 5

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2b.3–2b.10 · 2c.2–2c.4, 2c.6, 2c.10

CORE PRINCIPLE

Stabilise disease first; choose a maintainable option that fits the patient’s prognosis and priorities.

01 The five-phase plan

Urgent relief of pain or infection → stabilisation of periodontal/caries risk → re-evaluation → definitive restoration or replacement → supportive maintenance. A plan that starts with definitive crowns before disease control is usually unsound.

02 Compare options on common terms

For a missing unit, consider leaving the space, resin-bonded bridge, conventional bridge, removable prosthesis or implant-supported treatment when appropriate. Discuss tooth preparation, reversibility, aesthetics, cost, longevity, cleaning and failure consequences.

03 Conformative versus reorganised

Conform to a stable, comfortable existing intercuspal position where space and function permit. Reorganisation of occlusion, changes in OVD or complex multi-unit rehabilitation require careful diagnostic testing and often specialist involvement.

04 Consent is patient-specific

The supplied F Pros text references Montgomery: explain material risks and reasonable alternatives, including no treatment. The best choice is not necessarily the most technically elaborate option.

05 Communicate the sequence

Referral or laboratory instructions should contain the diagnosis, key-tooth prognosis, agreed phases, responsibilities, provisional plan, material/design choices and review arrangements.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

NHS restorative standards distinguish moderate Level 2 planning from complex full-mouth/MDT Level 3 care.

Source material: F Pros pp. 13–15 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 5: Periodontitis staging, grading and prognosis
pages.html:
Periodontitis staging, grading and prognosis

ASSESSMENT AND DIAGNOSIS

CORE PRINCIPLE

Stage reflects disease severity and complexity; grade reflects likely progression and modifies risk. Record stability separately.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Worst interproximal bone loss in coronal thirdOften stage I/II depending on degree of destructionConfirm CAL, tooth loss due to periodontitis and complexity
Bone loss extends into middle third of rootUsually supports Stage III assessmentReview deep pockets, vertical defects, furcation and tooth loss
Functional collapse, occlusal problems or very severe lossMay move case to Stage IV complexityInterdisciplinary rehabilitation and specialist input often needed
Bone loss/age ratio; cigarettes; glycaemic controlEvidence of progression and grade modifiersAvoid assigning grade solely from patient age

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

UK BSP implementation uses stage I-IV, grade A-C, extent, current stability and risk factors. Severe early-onset cases with palmoplantar keratosis (Papillon-Lefevre) or recurrent infections and pigment change (Chediak-Higashi) warrant syndromic assessment. A previously treated patient remains a periodontitis patient after therapy. Residual bleeding and pockets determine ongoing stability, not a reduction in historical stage.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A 40-year-old with bone loss near the middle third and heavy smoking cannot be classified by pocket depth alone. First determine stage using historical destruction and complexity, then assess grading evidence and modifiers.

EXAM TRAP

Do not call every rapidly progressing case "aggressive periodontitis"; the contemporary system has integrated it into staging and grading.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 5: Furcations, secondary occlusal trauma and molar prognosis
pages.html:
Furcations, secondary occlusal trauma and molar prognosis

ASSESSMENT AND DIAGNOSIS

CORE PRINCIPLE

A mobile molar can have multiple interacting causes. The decision is whether control of disease and load can make the tooth maintainable.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Grade II furcation on a stable molarHorizontal partial penetration with limited accessAssess debridement access, root anatomy and maintenance
Through-and-through furcation Complexity and cleansability reduce prognosisEvaluate root morphology, caries and regenerative/resective referral
Mobility with reduced periodontal supportSecondary occlusal trauma may increase mobilityTreat inflammatory disease and assess occlusal loading
Persistent pocket with negative sensibility testPossible endo-perio defect or vertical root fractureUse multiple investigations before extraction or splinting

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Excessive occlusal force can produce mobility, fremitus and widened periodontal ligament space but is not a substitute explanation for plaque-induced attachment loss. Prognosis incorporates furcation, residual support, restorability, patient factors and ability to clean the area.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A severely furcated molar with limited hygiene access and repeated abscesses may merit extraction discussion; a stable Grade II lesion with adequate plaque control can have a different maintenance plan.

EXAM TRAP

Splinting may improve comfort but does not reverse periodontal infection or make an unrestorable tooth sound.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 5: Endo-periodontal lesions: trace the original disease
pages.html:
Endo-periodontal lesions: trace the original disease

ASSESSMENT AND DIAGNOSIS

CORE PRINCIPLE

Pulp sensibility, pocket pattern, imaging and the history of restorative or traumatic injury often separate primary endodontic disease from a periodontal or combined lesion.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Non-vital tooth; isolated narrow draining tractPrimary endodontic origin more likelyTrace sinus and assess apical source; treat canal if restorable
Vital tooth; multiple broad pockets and bone lossPrimary periodontal process more likelyTreat biofilm and risk factors, reassess pulp as needed
Non-vital tooth with established widespread periodontitisTrue combined endo-periodontal involvement possibleEvaluate remaining attachment and restorability; staged approach
Very isolated deep pocket with J-shaped radiolucencyConsider vertical root fracture Inspect restoration/post, crack, probing and imaging limits

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Interpret sensibility tests with controls and limitations: calcified teeth may give false negative responses, and a single reading cannot establish histological necrosis. Compare pocket morphology and the radiographic pattern, looking for perforation or root damage before committing to treatment.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A tooth with an isolated sinus tract and normal adjacent periodontium is not managed like a vital molar with generalised bone loss. Treat the source and allow healing before deciding on extensive periodontal surgery.

EXAM TRAP

The old "primary with secondary involvement" labels are useful as explanatory mechanisms but are not a replacement for modern case-specific diagnosis.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 5: Pulpal pain, cracked tooth and referred TMD pain
pages.html:
Pulpal pain, cracked tooth and referred TMD pain

ASSESSMENT AND DIAGNOSIS

CORE PRINCIPLE

Test response, symptoms, percussion, biting and radiographic findings together; pain intensity alone is not a pulpal diagnosis.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Brief cold sensitivity resolving immediatelyCompatible with reversible pulpitis/dentine sensitivityAssess caries, exposure and reversible irritants
Spontaneous or lingering thermal painSymptomatic irreversible pulpitis more likelyEvaluate restorability and definitive pulp treatment options
Pain on release of bite; one cusp implicatedCracked tooth pattern Transillumination/bite test, periodontal probing, assess crack extent
Diffuse muscular pain; tooth tests normalPossible myofascial/TMD referral Reversible management and reassessment; avoid unnecessary RCT

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Apical periodontitis may present with percussion pain and may or may not have a visible radiolucency. Vitality and periapical diagnosis should be expressed separately. A split tooth, vertical root fracture and incomplete coronal crack have different prognoses.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A heavily restored premolar hurts when biting on one cusp but responds normally to cold. A cuspal crack is more plausible than irreversible pulpitis, and provisional cuspal protection may help while prognosis is assessed.

EXAM TRAP

Do not diagnose pulp necrosis solely because a heavily calcified or traumatised tooth fails a single cold test.

UNIT 6 Removable partial dentures

IN ONE MINUTE

Saddles, support, retention, bracing, connection, review — and design every free-end saddle for m ovem ent.

Surveying defines one path of insertion;

guide planes 2–4 mm parallel to it.

Rest seats: floor under 90°, 1–1.5 mm deep, cut after the guide planes.

Lingual bar needs 7–8 mm of functional sulcus; otherw ise a plate.

The dentist is responsible for the design; the laboratory prescription must specify every component. A w ell-designed, tooth-

supported cobalt–chrom ium R P Dina patient with good hygiene and regular recall does little harm to the remaining teeth (B ergm an); mucosa-borne acrylic dentures with gingival coverage do.

6.1 Design sequence

Saddles: outline the edentulous areas to be restored (consider the shortened dental arch — not every space needs filling).

Support: tooth (rests), mucosa (saddle and palate coverage), or both.

Retention: direct (clasps, guide planes, attachm ents) and indirect.

Bracing and reciprocation: resist lateral forces; reciprocal arms and guide planes.

Connection: major and minor connectors.

Review : simplify, m inim ise gingival coverage, check aesthetics and hygiene.

The three forces to resist: displacem ent towards the tissues (support), away from the tissues (retention), and lateral (bracing).

6.2 Surveying

Surveyor parts: vertical analysing rod, carbon marker (survey line), undercut gauges (0.25, 0.5, 0.75 mm ), wax trimm er.

Survey line = greatest convexity of a tooth relative to the chosen path of insertion. Undercut lies gingival to it.

Path of insertion is chosen by: guide planes, retention (suitable undercuts), interference (avoid hard and soft tissue undercuts that block insertion), and aesthetics (m inim ise visible clasp metal, allow anterior teeth to fit without gaps).

Path of displacem ent is assum ed perpendicular to the occlusal plane; retention needs the path of insertion to differ from it

(guide planes plus clasps).

Tilt: lowering the front of the cast (heels up) tips the crowns m esially relative to the vertical rod and increases m esial undercuts; lowering the heels increases distal undercuts. Record the tilt by tripoding the cast so the laboratory can reproduce it.

Guide planes: parallel proxim al surfaces 2–4 mm high prepared in enamel (or built into crow ns) parallel to the path of insertion; they define a single path, aid retention by friction, provide bracing and reduce food trapping.

Height of contour may need modifying by enam eloplasty (low er it) or composite (create an undercut or a rest seat).

6.3 Rests

Function: support (transm it occlusal load along the long axis), maintain the vertical position of the denture, prevent gingival im pingem ent, keep clasps in position, act as indirect retainers, prevent over-eruption.

6.6 Indirect retention

Fulcrum line: line through the rests nearest to the free-end saddles (or through the principal abutm ents).

A force pulling the saddle away from the ridge (sticky food) rotates the denture about this line; an indirect retainer placed as far anterior to the fulcrum line as possible resists it.

Examples: rests on canines or prem olars, cingulum rests, lingual plate, palatal plate extension anteriorly.

Indirect retainers also give support for an anterior extension and prevent the major connector settling.

pages.title: S07 | RPD design: applying the sequence
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 6 → Diploma Unit 6

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2c.2–2c.6, 2c.13, 2c.20

CORE PRINCIPLE

Start from the saddle and support; only then choose clasps, connector and indirect retention.

01 Design in order

Saddles → support → retention → bracing/reciprocation → major connectors → indirect retention → review. Identify Kennedy class after extractions; a distal-extension RPD needs tooth-and-mucosa support.

02 Biomechanical consequences

Mesial rests and stress-releasing concepts may reduce torque on distal-extension abutments. Survey casts, establish the insertion path and create suitable guide planes and rest seats before taking the definitive impression.

03 Numbers worth interpreting

The F Pros source gives a common 0.25 mm Co-Cr undercut and approximately 0.5 mm for cast gold/wrought wire. A lingual bar generally needs adequate functional sulcus depth, approximately 7–8 mm between the gingival margin and floor of mouth; otherwise consider a lingual plate.

04 Common failures

Pain after fitting may arise from overextension, tissue pressure or a high rest seat. Distal-extension saddles lose support as the ridge changes; assess the need for reline rather than merely tightening a clasp.

05 Exam trap

A retentive clasp without effective reciprocation is not a complete design. Choosing a clasp before assessing support and insertion path reverses the design logic.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Framework design must be individualized to teeth, anatomy and support; numerical rules are approximate.

Source material: F Pros pp. 21–23 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 6: RPD biomechanics: support before clasp retention
pages.html:
RPD biomechanics: support before clasp retention

REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

For a distal-extension saddle, the support tissues move differently: tooth-supported rests resist displacement, while mucosa can compress and rotate the base.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Kennedy Class I/II free-end saddleDifferential tooth and tissue displacementBroad base coverage, mesial rests and controlled stress release
Short distal base and terminal clasp on tilted toothLevering increases load on abutmentResurvey path, rests, guide planes and clasp design
Deep undercut on weak or highly mobile abutmentRetentive force may be excessive Reduce demand or redesign with indirect retention/support
Long-span major connector or flexible baseFlexure compromises distribution and reciprocationProvide adequate rigidity, hygiene and clearance

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The framework should resist displacement towards tissues (rests and base), away from tissues (retentive arm and indirect retention), and laterally (bracing and reciprocation). A retentive clasp is not an adequate substitute for properly placed rests and a rigid major connector.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A Kennedy I patient repeatedly loosens a clasp after adding a thin distal acrylic saddle. The first priority is not a stiffer clasp: assess extension, support, rotation axis, rest position and occlusion.

EXAM TRAP

In a free-end saddle, an excessively rigid distal clasp can torque the abutment during tissueward movement.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 6: Altered-cast impression: procedure and indication
pages.html:
Altered-cast impression: procedure and indication

REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

The altered-cast technique aims to record the distal-extension mucosa under a selected functional condition while preserving the tooth-supported framework relationship.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Indication: distal-extension RPDTooth and mucosal support are dissimilarConsider altered cast where clinically useful and technically feasible
Framework trial before final impressionStable rests and complete seating requiredVerify passivity, rests, guide planes and occlusal clearance
Custom tray attached to seated frameworkAccurate impression of saddle-bearing tissuesBorder mould, apply chosen impression technique and control pressure
Master cast modified after impressionDistal saddle section replaced using secured frameworkReseat framework precisely; pour altered section without displacement

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Sequence: make accurate master cast; survey/design and fabricate Co-Cr framework; verify full framework seating intraorally; attach/assess saddle trays; border-mould and record tissues with framework held in position; section the original edentulous cast portions; seat the framework and impression on remaining tooth portions; box and pour new saddle anatomy.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

If the framework itself rocks on the rests at trial, an altered cast will reproduce a false relationship. Correct the framework or its cast before attempting to compensate with impression material.

EXAM TRAP

This is not simply "a mucocompressive impression": pressure distribution, tray relief and correct framework seating remain essential.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 6: Flexible RPD versus sectional denture
pages.html:
Flexible RPD versus sectional denture

REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

The selection should solve the anatomical insertion problem while retaining adequate support, hygiene and future adjustability.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Severe single-sided undercut prevents conventional insertionSectional denture with planned joining mechanismSelect when segments can seat on distinct paths and be stabilised
Mild undercuts and high aesthetic demandPotential indication for flexible polymer base/claspEvaluate support, replaceability, repair and tissue loading
Bilateral lingual tori with poor lingual connector clearanceConsider surgical modification or labial/sublingual alternativeDo not force a lingual bar over the tori
Lingually tilted posterior teeth obstruct insertionSurvey interference and path before deciding denture typeModify design/teeth if justified rather than defaulting to flexible

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Flexible polyamide is not equivalent to a sectional denture. A sectional design is selected for a controlled two-part insertion/removal pathway when a one-piece framework cannot be safely inserted; its attachments and stability may be technique-sensitive. Flexible bases may mask insertion issues but often offer less rigid support and more difficult modification.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A lower arch has missing anterior teeth and severely lingually inclined posterior teeth. Evaluate survey lines, guiding surfaces and the intended path first. Only if a single insertion path is not feasible should a sectional option enter the leading choices.

EXAM TRAP

A flexible denture without rest support can direct repeated tissueward force onto the residual ridge.

pages.html:
Co-Cr RPD laboratory sequence and failure localisation

REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

The laboratory procedure board must connect clinical design with fabrication quality controls.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Survey and prescription Path of insertion, blockout and rest seats define designIdentify undercuts and components before sending to laboratory
Duplicate and refractory cast Expansion/accuracy must suit Co-Cr frameworkCheck impression duplication and refractory investment integrity
Wax pattern, sprues and castingPorosity, incomplete fill or distortion can developInspect critical connectors, clasps, rests and casting surfaces
Finishing, polishing and framework try-inOvergrinding changes strength and retentionVerify passive seating, rest contact, reciprocation and tissue clearance

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

There is no single universally highest-failure step: errors can occur at impression, block-out, pattern handling, spruing, investment, burnout, casting or finishing. Distinguish a framework that does not fit the master cast (laboratory issue) from one that fits the cast but not the patient (cast/impression or clinical change).

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A Co-Cr clasp tip is short and poorly formed while the rest and connector fit: suspect local casting or finishing. A framework whose rests all fail to seat intraorally despite perfect cast fit: reassess impression and master-cast accuracy.

EXAM TRAP

Ask the technician to document alloy, casting method and repairability; never adjust a connector until design and fit have been checked.

pages.html:
Lower posterior occlusal plane at about tw o-thirds the height of the retrom olar pad and level with the lateral border of the tongue at rest.

Centre line coincides with the facial midline (philtrum ); canine lines at the corners of the mouth at rest; high lip (sm ile) line shows the necessary length of the teeth.

7.4 Vertical dimension

Rest vertical dimension (R V D ) − occlusal vertical dimension (O V D ) = freew ay space (interocclusal rest space), normally 2–

4 mm (average about 3 mm ).

Measuring: Willis gauge (base of nose to underside of chin; Willis noted pupil-to-stom ion distance roughly equals nose-to- chin), dividers on dots, existing dentures, phonetics (closest speaking space about 1–2 mm on "s"), appearance, swallow ing.

Rest position is not fixed: affected by head posture, fatigue, emotion, dentures in or out — measure several times with the patient upright and relaxed.

O V D TO OH IG H (FR EEWAYSPACE TO OSMA LL) O V D TO O LOW (FR EEWAYSPACE TO OLA R G E )

G eneralised soreness of the denture-bearing area, especially the lower ridge Angular cheilitis (folding at the comm issures)

Teeth click during speech A ged, "collapsed" appearance; prominent chin

Strained appearance, lips apart at rest Reduced m asticatory efficiency

Fatigue of m asticatory muscles; difficulty eating Cheek biting (cheeks fold between the teeth)

Faster ridge resorption Tongue may seem crowded

7.5 Horizontal jaw relation

Complete dentures are made in the retruded contact position (R C P ) because it is reproducible; IC P is coincident with it in the finished dentures.

Recording: guide the mandible gently to the retruded arc with the patient relaxed and the tongue curled back; check that the blocks meet evenly without sliding.

Gothic arch (needle-point) tracer: the apex of the arrow head marks R C P ; useful when registration is unreliable.

Errors in R C P show at try-in as posterior teeth not meeting evenly, or a slide. Take a new registration and re-articulate rather than adjusting teeth.

7.6 A rticulators and occlusion

Simple hinge: no lateral m ovem ent, ignore.

Average value: fixed condylar guidance (about 30°) and B onw ill triangle (about 10 cm sides); adequate for most complete dentures.

S em i-adjustable (arcon or non-arcon): condylar guidance set from a protrusive record; Bennett angle often from H anau's

formula L = H /8 + 12; used with a facebow .

A rcon: condylar element on the lower member, anatom ically correct (W hip Mix, D enar). N on-arcon: condylar element on the

upper member (D entatus, H anau H2).

Lingualised occlusion: only upper palatal cusps contact the lower central fossae; good stability with resorbed ridges and acceptable aesthetics.

Monoplane (zero-degree) teeth: least horizontal force; for severely resorbed ridges, Class III relationships, poor neurom uscular control.

7.7 Tooth selection and setting

Anterior width: canine lines and inter-alar width; central incisor width about one-sixteenth of bizygom atic width (B erry). William s' face-form theory and Frush and Fisher's dentogenics (sex, personality, age) guide shape butare weakly evidence-

based.

Shade: darker and with characterisation for older patients; involve the patient; avoid very light "denture look".

Lower posterior teeth over the ridge crest and in the neutral zone; never on the ascending slope of the ramus (the denture would be pushed forw ard).

Upper posterior teeth may sit buccal to a resorbed maxillary ridge; set in crossbite where the maxilla is much narrow er than

the mandible.

Neutral zone: area where tongue forces balance lip and cheek forces; record with tissue conditioner, impression compound or soft wax on a lower base during function (sw allow ing, speaking). Most useful for resorbed lower ridges and previously unstable lower dentures.

Posterior horizontal overlap (buccal overjet) prevents cheek biting.

P ost-dam : on the upper master cast, along the vibrating line from ham ular notch to ham ular notch, deepest (about 1–1.5 mm ) either side of the midline, shallow er over the median raphe. Functions: posterior seal, compensates for polym erisation contraction lifting the posterior border, reduces food entry and gagging.

Vibrating line marked by asking the patient to say "ah"; the V alsalva m anoeuvre identifies the anterior vibrating line.

A clinical rem ount (new R C P record on the processed dentures, rem ounted on the articulator) corrects occlusal errors from processing more accurately than adjusting in the mouth.

7.10 Special complete denture techniques

Copy (replica) dentures: duplicate the polished and occlusal surfaces of dentures the patient has adapted to, changing only what is necessary (fitting surface, O V D , occlusion). Best for older patients with poor adaptive capacity. The replica (w ax teeth on shellac or acrylic base) acts as special tray and record block.

Immediate dentures: flanged (better retention, stability and reline potential) vs open-face (socketed; better emergence appearance but poor retention and cannot be relined labially). Teeth are removed from the cast and the sockets lightly trimm ed. Leave in for the first 24 hours; review next day; reline at about 3–6 months; replace later as resorption continues.

O verdentures: retained roots (canines are ideal — longest roots, strategic position) reduced to 2–3 mm above the gingiva with domed surfaces and root fillings; preserve bone and proprioception, improve support, retention with attachm ents. Risks: caries and periodontitis — fluoride gel in the denture fitting surface, meticulous hygiene.

Implant overdentures: M cG ill consensus (2002) and York consensus (2009): a tw o-im plant mandibular overdenture should be

the m inim um standard of care for the edentulous mandible.

Single complete denture against natural teeth: risk of fracture and of combination syndrom e (K elly): anterior maxillary resorption and flabby ridge, tuberosity enlargem ent, papillary hyperplasia, over-eruption of lower anteriors, resorption under lower free-end saddles. Prevent by restoring posterior support (low erR P D ) and reducing anterior loading.

Flabby ridge impressions: mucostatic (im pression plaster) or selective pressure (w indow ed special tray: m ucocom pressive material for the firm ridge, then low -viscosity material or plaster through the window over the flabby tissue).

R eline (new fitting surface) vs rebase (w hole base replaced). C hairside hard reline is quick but more porous; closed-mouth

laboratory reline can increase O V Dif the patient bites too firmly.

P re-prosthetic surgery (tuberosity reduction, vestibuloplasty, torus rem oval) is usually Level 3.

Examiner traps — Unit 7

Clicking teeth and generalised soreness mean the O V Dis too high.

A n upper denture that drops on wide opening points to the distobuccal flange and the coronoid.

The occlusal plane is parallel to the interpupillary line anteriorly and to Cam per's plane posteriorly.

The tw o-im plant overdenture is the m inim um standard for the edentulous mandible.

pages.title: S08 | Complete dentures: stability and adaptation
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 6 → Diploma Unit 7

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2c.4, 2c.9, 2c.13, 2c.19, 2c.21–2c.27

CORE PRINCIPLE

Retention is only one part of success: harmony with the neutral zone and the patient’s adaptation is equally important.

01 Clinical sequence

Primary impressions → special trays → border-moulded secondary impressions → occlusal rims and jaw registration → trial dentures → insertion → review. Recheck each step instead of hoping the technician will compensate for a faulty record.

02 Choose an impression strategy

Displace flabby tissue as little as clinically appropriate; selective pressure or a window technique may help. Functional borders and the posterior palatal seal have to be assessed clinically.

03 Occlusal scheme and OVD

The source summarises OVD as rest vertical dimension minus roughly 2–4 mm of freeway space. In severely resorbed ridges, lingualised or carefully balanced occlusion and a neutral-zone approach may improve stability.

04 Patient adaptation

For older patients with successful old dentures, copy techniques preserve useful adaptation while changing only identified defects. Explain the likely need for early relines with immediate dentures and the adjustment period following insertion.

05 Exam trap

Increasing vertical dimension or adding more adhesive rarely cures an overextended flange, inaccurate border, unstable record or incorrect neutral-zone position.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Discuss implant-assisted dentures as an option or referral; specialist implant surgery is not a Level 2 learning requirement.

Source material: F Pros pp. 21–23 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)
