pages.html:
Flabby and atrophic ridges: functional impression choice

COMPLETE DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

An impression should preserve tissue form and record useful support without displacing tissue that rebounds after insertion.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Mobile anterior maxillary ridge Selective pressure/window or mucostatic recordingMinimise distortion over flabby area; use stable palate for support
Flat mandibular ridge with limited attached mucosaFunctionally shaped borders and broad supportAssess retromylohyoid and buccal shelf before increasing OVD
Denture sore spots despite good static fitDynamic border overextension or occlusal traumaMap pressure under functional movements
Rigid impression material in deep undercutsRemoval trauma and distortion riskChoose appropriate elastomer or block out as indicated

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Mucostatic approaches record tissue with minimal displacement; mucocompressive approaches intentionally load selected tissues; selective-pressure approaches combine support and relief. No single impression material alone guarantees the physiological pressure state - tray design and operator control matter.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

An upper complete denture is unstable because mobile anterior ridge tissue was compressed during the wash impression. A windowed or selective-pressure technique is preferable to simply increasing posterior palatal seal pressure.

EXAM TRAP

Do not confuse an under-extended lingual flange with a need for a longer occlusal vertical dimension.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 7: Neutral zone, jaw relations and vertical dimension
pages.html:
Neutral zone, jaw relations and vertical dimension

COMPLETE DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

A jaw-registration number is a cross-check, not a substitute for repeatable mandibular positioning and evaluation of facial comfort.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Severely resorbed lower ridge, unstable trial rimMuscle balance can dominate denture stabilityRecord neutral zone; shape polished surface and tooth position
Altered mandibular posture or neuromuscular diseaseRVD and repeatability can be unreliableUse several methods and patient-specific reproducibility checks
Excessive OVD Lip strain, clicking, speaking difficulty, muscle fatigueRecheck jaw relation and interocclusal rest space
Insufficient OVD Overclosure, reduced facial support and altered functionVerify before raising the bite; consider existing adaptation

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The conventional rest space is approximately 2-4 mm in many patients but varies individually. Record and verify centric relation, interocclusal distance, phonetics, facial support and comfort; copy records may help when adaptation is poor. Neutral-zone recording can be done with mouldable material over a stable base while the patient swallows and speaks.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A new lower denture repeatedly dislodges during speech despite a well-fitting base on a flat ridge. Reassess tooth position and polished-surface contour within the neutral zone before proposing an implant solely because the ridge is flat.

EXAM TRAP

A single RVD minus a fixed 3-mm value is not a sufficient method to prescribe OVD for every patient.

pages.html:
Try-in: phonetics, facial planes and bite checks

COMPLETE DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

Try-in is the point to test the proposed tooth position and jaw relation against speech, aesthetics, comfort and mandibular movement.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
F and V sounds; upper incisal edgesIncisal edges relate to the lower lip wet-dry borderAdjust length and labiolingual position, not just shade
Sibilants and closest speaking spaceExcess contact or large gap can indicate errorCheck anterior relation and vertical dimension together
Occlusal plane wax rim Facial plane references aid orientationUse interpupillary line/frontal aesthetics and ala-tragus as guides
Frankfort horizontal (porion-orbitale)Reference in cephalometry and facebow orientationNot a direct stand-alone rule for denture tooth positions

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Use multiple recordings when the patient cannot repeat jaw closure: stable bases, tracing where indicated, guided closure and assessment of existing dentures. Verify centric contacts and excursions; document any deliberate changes to the established occlusion. Speech tests should use the patient's normal language and conversational rate.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A trial denture looks acceptable but S sounds whistle and the teeth contact during speaking. The more useful response is to check anterior tooth position and closest speaking space, not immediately reduce posterior cusps.

EXAM TRAP

The Frankfort horizontal reference does not replace chairside checks of smile line, occlusal plane and lip support.

pages.html:
UNIT 8 Fixed prosthodontics

N um ber card 3

IN ONE MINUTE

Taper, height and ferrule holda crown on; A nte's law and the cube of the span decide a bridge.

Margins supragingival where possible,

and at least 3 mm from the bone crest.

For sound abutm ents with good enamel, a resin-bonded cantilever is the first choice.

In ceram ic connectors, height matters more than width.

Fixed bridge design was examined last sitting: be fluent in abutm ent evaluation, choosing between fixed-fixed, cantilever, fixed- movable and resin-bonded designs, pontic forms and the mechanics of span and connectors.

8.1 Principles of tooth preparation (S hillingburg)

Preservation of tooth structure (and pulp).

Retention and resistance form .

Structural durability of the restoration (adequate material thickness, functional cusp bevel).

Marginal integrity.

Preservation of the periodontium .

Taper (total occlusal convergence): theoretical ideal about 6°; clinically 10–20° is typical and acceptable. Retention falls sharply as convergence increases.

M inim um axial wall height: about 3 mm for incisors and prem olars, 4 mm for m olars. H eight-to-w idth ratio of at least 0.4

improves resistance.

Short or over-tapered preparations: add grooves or boxes, increase surface area, use adhesive cem ents, consider crown lengthening (Level 3 surgery) or elective endodontics with a core only as a last resort.

Pulp protection: sharp burs, copious water spray, light interm ittent pressure, avoid desiccation, w ell-fitting temporaries;

dentine sealing.

8.3 Margins and the periodontium

Prefer supragingival margins (hygiene, impression, finishing, inspection). E quigingival or slightly subgingival only for aesthetics, caries, existing restorations, ferrule or retention.

S upracrestal tissue attachm ent ("biologic w idth") averages about 2 mm (connective tissue about 1 mm plus junctional

epithelium about 1 mm ; G argiulo); with the sulcus, keep margins about 3 mm from the bone crest. Invasion causes chronic

inflam mation, recession or bone loss.

O vercontoured crowns (especially in furcation areas) trap plaque: keep emergence profiles flat.

Gingival retraction: plain or impregnated cord (alum inium chloride or ferric sulphate; avoid adrenaline cord in cardiovascular disease), double-cord technique, retraction pastes, electrosurgery or laser.

8.4 Temporary (provisional) restorations

Purposes: protect the pulp, maintain tooth position (prevent drift and over-eruption), protect gingival health, restore function

and aesthetics, test the planned shape, O V D or occlusion.

Materials: bis-acryl composite (low exotherm , good strength, comm on); PMMA (stronger for long-term but exotherm ic and higher residual m onom er); prefabricated polycarbonate or metal crowns.

Use eugenol-free temporary cement if the definitive restoration will be resin-bonded.

8.5 Occlusion, shade and impressions

Conform ative approach (m ost single units and short bridges): restore to the existing IC P without changing the occlusal

schem e.

R eorganised approach (R C P /centric relation): when IC P is unstable, extensive restoration is planned, or O V D will change.

Usually Level 3 when major.

Shade: take before preparation (teeth dehydrate and lighten during treatm ent), in colour-corrected daylight, quickly; value is the most important dimension; photograph with shade tabs and send to the laboratory.

Impressions: addition silicone or polyether in a rigid tray; dual-arch (triple) trays only for single units with stable intercuspation. Intraoral scans suit short-span work.

Die spacer (about 20–40 µm ) gives room for cement; it stops short of the margin.

8.6 E ndodontically treated teeth

Posterior root-filled teeth need cuspal coverage (onlay or crow n) — survival improves markedly (S orensen and M artinoff); anterior root-filled teeth with little tissue loss can be restored with composite.

Ferrule of 1.5–2 mm of sound dentine is the most important factor in fracture resistance ( Section 3.13 for post rules).

Posts retain cores; they do not strengthen roots.

M olars: amalgam or composite core retained in the pulp chamber (N ayyar core) without a post is often enough.

Provide a good coronal seal promptly after root canal treatm ent; coronal leakage contributes to failure.

A nte's law : the total root surface area of the abutm ents should equal or exceed that of the teeth being replaced. It is historical and not well supported by evidence, but still examined.

Relative root surface area (largest to sm allest): maxilla 6 > 7 > 3 > 4 ≈ 5 > 1 > 2; mandible 6 > 7 > 3 > 5 ≈ 4 > 2 > 1. Upper canine has the largest root of the single-rooted teeth.

Span mechanics: deflection of a beam increases with the cube of its length and decreases with the cube of its thickness (occluso-gingival connector height). Doubling the span gives about eight times the flexure.

Arch curvature: pontics lying outside the line joining the abutm ents (e.g., replacing all four upper incisors) act as a lever arm causing torque.

pages.title: S09 | Fixed prosthodontics: preparation to review
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 5 → Diploma Unit 8

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2c.2, 2c.4, 2c.6, 2c.11, 2c.13–2c.14

CORE PRINCIPLE

Preserve sound tooth structure and select a restoration with adequate retention, resistance and long-term hygiene.

01 Preparation principles

Compare partial coverage, onlay/overlay, resin-bonded bridge and full crown. Verify clearance, marginal design, axial wall height, taper and ferrule rather than treating one preparation number as a universal rule.

02 Use the right adhesive chemistry

The F Pros notes contrast silica-based ceramics requiring silane-based bonding with zirconia requiring alternative surface conditioning/MDP approaches. A cement cannot compensate for poor resistance form.

03 Biological protection

Deep reduction, heat, desiccation and provisional leakage can damage the pulp. Subgingival overcontours and poor emergence profiles increase plaque retention and soft-tissue inflammation.

04 Bridge design choices

Review span, abutment periodontal support, tooth preservation, patient cleaning ability and the feasibility of a cantilever resin-bonded design. More retainers are not automatically safer.

05 Success is more than survival

At recall inspect biological health, contacts, margins, caries, cracks, occlusion, aesthetics and patient satisfaction. Parafunction may change material and maintenance choices.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Full-mouth reconstruction and complex occlusal reorganisation are Level 3/referral scenarios, not routine Diploma execution.

Source material: F Pros pp. 18–20 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.title: S10 | Aesthetic dentistry: least invasive first
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 10 → Diploma Unit 8

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2a.16 · 2b.6, 2b.10 · 2c.4

CORE PRINCIPLE

Start with a systematic assessment of the smile, then solve the patient’s actual concern using the least destructive option.

01 Analyse from outside inward

Facial symmetry and midline → lip support/smile line → incisal display and occlusal plane → tooth proportions, shade, gingival contour and papillae. A mathematical “golden proportion” is not a mandatory natural smile rule.

02 Treatment ladder

For colour: investigate aetiology and consider whitening first. For white spots: consider infiltration or microabrasion. For spacing or peg laterals: consider additive composite; for malalignment: orthodontics before elective tooth preparation.

03 Before an indirect veneer

Use diagnostic wax-up/mock-up, assess enamel availability, parafunction and deep overbite, and discuss irreversibility and long-term replacement. Whitening may alter the final shade and immediate resin bonding conditions.

04 Patient-centred consent

Discuss maintenance, failure, costs and reasonable alternatives including no treatment. Distinguish a realistic restorative concern from expectations that cannot safely be met.

05 SBA trap

A crown on an otherwise healthy tooth for a minor aesthetic complaint is generally less conservative than whitening, orthodontics or additive composite if those can meet the objective.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Complex gingival/orthognathic procedures require appropriate specialist assessment, not Diploma-level operative detail.

Source material: F Pros pp. 31–32 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 8: Crown margin and reduction: material-specific reasoning
pages.html:
Crown margin and reduction: material-specific reasoning

FIXED PROSTHODONTICS

CORE PRINCIPLE

Preparation is determined by restorative material thickness, finish-line compatibility, available tooth structure and periodontal health.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Metal-ceramic/PFM crown: porcelain-bearing surfaceAdequate reduction and rounded support neededOften a shoulder/heavy chamfer for porcelain; material-specific design
Metal-only margin Conservative chamfer may be suitableAvoid under-reduction and thin unsupported metal
Glass-ceramic adhesive restorationRounded internal geometry and adequate ceramic bulkFollow ceramic and bonding system requirements
Knife-edge/feather-edge finish linePotentially appropriate for selected metal situationsPoor choice for ceramics needing identifiable bulk; difficult control

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Indicative figures differ between systems: many conventional metal-ceramic preparations use approximately 1.2-1.5 mm on porcelain-bearing axial surfaces and 1.5-2 mm occlusally/incisally where porcelain is present; monolithic materials may permit other dimensions. Use the selected manufacturer's values, not an exam-wide universal number.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A short clinical crown has limited axial wall height but is being prepared for a ceramic PFM margin. Improving resistance form and preserving sound tissue may be more important than automatically extending a deep subgingival shoulder.

EXAM TRAP

A biologic tissue attachment violation cannot be corrected simply by polishing the margin or prescribing chlorhexidine.

Retention, resistance and bridge failure

FIXED PROSTHODONTICS

CORE PRINCIPLE

A crown or bridge may fail despite adequate cement because the geometry cannot resist displacement or rotation.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Short, wide preparation with large taperPoor resistance to oblique displacementImprove geometry, grooves/boxes or consider alternative restorative plan
Long-span conventional bridge Deflection rises steeply with span lengthAssess abutment support, connector size, pontic position and load
Two-wing resin-bonded bridge with unilateral debondSilent caries risk under partially detached retainerConsider single-retainer cantilever and moisture/bond control
Repeated porcelain chipping on bridgeUnsupported ceramic or excursive contactReview framework support, ceramic thickness and guidance

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Retention resists withdrawal approximately along the path of insertion; resistance prevents oblique tipping/rotation. The prognosis also depends on ferrule where needed, remaining dentine, occlusal loading and periodontal status. For RBBs, enamel bonding area, rigid connector and isolation are frequently more decisive than adding another retainer.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A resin-bonded lateral-incisor replacement debonds on one of two retainers without mobility of the other. Recementing both wings without considering hidden leakage is less appropriate than redesigning the adhesive bridge and protecting abutment teeth.

EXAM TRAP

Ante's law and "span cubed" are planning prompts, not substitutes for individual bridge biomechanics.

pages.title: S11 | TMD: diagnosis, red flags and self-care
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 8 → Diploma Unit 9

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2a.15, 2a.20 · 2c.19

CORE PRINCIPLE

Most common TMD presentations should be assessed conservatively; not every jaw pain is TMD.

01 Classify rather than guess

Separate muscle-related pain, TMJ arthralgia and disc/displacement disorders using the history and examination; consider the DC/TMD framework. Document pain location, movement limitation, joint noise, locking and functional impact.

02 First-line management

Explain the condition, provide reassurance, self-care, soft diet during acute symptoms, habit awareness, controlled jaw exercise and appropriate analgesia. A reversible stabilisation splint may be useful in selected cases.

03 Avoid irreversible overtreatment

Occlusal adjustment, orthodontics and extensive restorative reconstructions are not default cures for TMD. Changing an otherwise stable occlusion for pain without a sound diagnosis is a common examiner trap.

04 Recognise red flags

Suspicious swelling, unexplained neurological signs, significant trauma, systemic inflammatory features, rapidly progressive restriction or atypical pain should trigger broader assessment and appropriate referral.

05 Imaging decisions

Routine imaging is not obligatory for typical uncomplicated muscle pain. Choose targeted imaging when the clinical question concerns bone pathology, structural change or an alternative diagnosis.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Persistent complex TMD, diagnostic uncertainty or closed lock not responding to conservative care is a referral issue.

Source material: F Pros pp. 27–28 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.html:
Occlusion across teeth, dentures and implants

OCCLUSION AND TMD

CORE PRINCIPLE

Occlusal scheme follows the supporting system: periodontal ligament, mucosa and osseointegrated implant tissues respond differently to load.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Dentate patient with healthy periodontal supportControlled intercuspation with functional guidanceExamine excursive contacts, symptoms and restoration design
Kennedy Class I RPD opposing teethSaddle rotation under function can destabilise prosthesisCoordinate base support, balanced contacts and clasp mechanics
Bilateral complete dentures Destabilising lateral contacts and tipping are criticalSelect an appropriate balanced or lingualised scheme
Implant crown/bridge or overdentureImplants lack conventional PDL proprioceptionAvoid uncontrolled cantilever and non-axial overload; monitor hardware

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

A non-working interference is not automatically pathogenic. Relate it to the patient's symptoms, wear, mobility, restorations and functional pattern. Irreversible equilibration is inappropriate as a routine primary treatment for nonspecific TMD. Bruxism may increase prosthetic complications but should not be equated with a diagnosis of TMD.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A complete denture tips during excursion on steep posterior cusps; contact adjustment may help. The same contact in a patient with natural dentition and no symptoms does not justify wholesale occlusal grinding.

EXAM TRAP

Stable occlusion is an outcome of support and anatomy, not merely a collection of articulating-paper marks.

pages.title: Unit 10: Tooth wear and failing dentition
pages.html:
UNIT 10 Tooth surface loss, the failing dentition and the perio–endo–pros interface

IN ONE MINUTE

S tabilise disease, prevent, then restore additively; the Dahl approach makes space without cutting tooth.

Phases: urgent → stabilisation → reassessm ent (50% im provem ent = engaging) → definitive → maintenance.

Know what is Level 2 and what is Level

3 under the N H S standard.

Decide restorability before root canal treatm ent.

Control disease and diagnose the cause before restoring: the N H S prosthodontic entry criteria require a stable oral environm ent (good hygiene, caries risk managed, active caries treated, periodontal disease stable).

10.1 Phased treatm ent planning

Urgent care: relief of pain and infection.

S tabilisation (hygiene phase): oral hygiene and diet advice, caries removal and tem porisation, periodontal steps 1–2, extraction of hopeless teeth, transitional or interim prostheses, smoking cessation and medical risk control.

R eassessm ent: response to stabilisation, motivation (plaque and bleeding scores — a 50% im provem ent indicates an engaging patient), prognosis of remaining teeth.

Definitive (corrective) phase: endodontics, periodontal surgery if needed, then fixed and removable prosthodontics.

Maintenance: recall interval matched to risk; supportive periodontal care; prosthesis review .

10.2 Managing tooth wear

Identify and remove the cause (diet diary, medical history for GORD and eating disorders, habits); refer to GM P for intrinsic

causes.

Prevention: reduce frequency of acidic intake and confine it to meals, drink through a straw , do not brush immediately after acid exposure, fluoride (high-concentration toothpaste, varnish), desensitising agents, night-tim e splint for bruxism .

Monitor: photographs, study casts, silicone indices, BEWE or S m ith and Knight scores.

Restore when there is pain or sensitivity, aesthetic or functional concern, structural compromise or pulpal risk, or docum ented progression despite prevention.

M inim al-intervention additive approach first: direct resin composite (repairable, adhesive, reversible), then indirect composite or gold or ceram ic onlays and palatal veneers; conventional crowns last (they remove more tooth).

10.3 The Dahl concept

Origin: Dahl (1975) used a removable cobalt–chrom ium anterior bite platform to create space for restoring worn upper anterior

teeth; today the same principle uses direct composite restorations placed at an increased O V D .

How it works: posterior teeth are initially out of contact. Over about 4–6 months (occasionally up to 18) occlusal contacts re- establish by a combination of intrusion of the anterior teeth and over-eruption (extrusion) of the posterior teeth, with some mandibular repositioning.

Best suited to localised anterior wear where compensatory dentoalveolar growth has removed interocclusal space.

pages.title: S12 | Tooth wear: prevention before rebuilding
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 9 → Diploma Unit 10

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 1.4, 1.8 · 2a.15, 2a.20 · 2c.10–2c.12

CORE PRINCIPLE

The exam tests the causes, progression and consequences of wear—not just how to create restorative space.

01 Identify the mechanism

Erosion is acid-mediated; attrition is tooth-to-tooth contact; abrasion is friction with an external object; abfraction is a debated stress-related model. Mixed lesions are common, so identify relevant risk factors and their frequency.

02 Establish whether to intervene

Record history, photos, charting and, where useful, BEWE or serial scans/casts. Assess dentine sensitivity, aesthetics, dento-alveolar compensation, pulp risk and whether wear is active.

03 Disease control and additive care

Manage dietary acid and reflux/eating-disorder concerns, optimise fluoride measures and monitor. For suitable localised anterior wear, Dahl-type relative axial movement can help gain space with additive restorations.

04 When rehabilitation is complex

Changes in OVD, unstable occlusion, severe generalised wear, reduced crown height or multiple failing restorations require a diagnostic wax-up, temporary testing and often specialist planning.

05 SBA traps

Do not infer reduced OVD from worn teeth alone. Do not plan full crowns before stabilising the cause of erosion or reviewing the amount of remaining tooth tissue.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

This covers recognition and planning. Specialist crown lengthening/reorganisation is a referral pathway when indicated.

Source material: F Pros pp. 29–30 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.title: S13 | Trauma: prosthodontic consequences
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 12 → Diploma Unit 10

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2a.7, 2a.9–2a.10, 2a.14, 2a.18 · 2c.10

CORE PRINCIPLE

F Pros includes a full trauma chapter; for the Diploma, focus on identification, urgent action, restorability and referral.

01 Emergency recognition

The source cites IADT 2020: replant an avulsed permanent tooth promptly if appropriate; never replant an avulsed primary tooth. If immediate replantation is not possible, preserve the tooth in an appropriate medium and arrange urgent expert care.

02 Longer-term complications

After trauma, monitor for pulpal necrosis, inflammatory or replacement resorption, ankylosis, colour changes and root fracture healing. Interpret radiographs and clinical signs together over time.

03 Plan around growth

An osseointegrated implant does not erupt with a growing jaw, so a fixed implant is generally deferred until growth is complete. Temporary tooth replacement or orthodontic options may preserve future choices.

04 Restorability principles

Consider sound tissue, root length, fracture position, periodontal support, ferrule and expected maintenance. A growing patient with complex traumatic injury merits multidisciplinary advice.

05 Limit of this supplement

Specific splint duration, repositioning techniques, pulpotomy and decoronation are treated in F Pros at specialist depth; they are not presented here as required Diploma operative competencies.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Use current IADT protocols in real emergencies and refer promptly. Trauma is contextual to the supplied Diploma outcomes.

Source material: F Pros pp. 35–36 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.html:
Dental trauma: what changes prognosis?

TOOTH WEAR AND FAILING DENTITION

CORE PRINCIPLE

For the examination, establish dentition, maturity of the root, displacement, contamination, extra-oral dry time and pulpal status before selecting treatment.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Uncomplicated crown fracture Enamel/dentine fracture without pulp exposureProtect dentine and restore; assess for luxation
Complicated crown fracture Pulp exposure; stage of root maturity mattersConsider vital pulp therapy versus RCT by case factors
Root fracture cervical/mid/apical thirdCoronal fragment displacement and stability differReposition/splint where indicated and monitor healing
Avulsed permanent tooth Extra-oral dry time and storage medium criticalUrgent evidence-based replantation pathway; never replant primary tooth

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The IADT guidance separates fractures and luxation injuries from avulsion. Assess additional alveolar fracture, percussion, mobility and soft-tissue foreign bodies, and arrange the recommended serial reviews. Pulp testing immediately after trauma may be inconclusive and requires repeat evaluation.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

An avulsed mature permanent incisor stored dry for over an hour has a much poorer periodontal ligament prognosis than one promptly replanted after suitable storage. Both require urgent professional management, but long-term risks and counselling differ.

EXAM TRAP

A discoloured traumatised tooth is not automatically necrotic - examine sensibility trends, periapical changes and canal obliteration.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 10: Tooth wear, cracked teeth and safe additive rehabilitation
pages.html:
Tooth wear, cracked teeth and safe additive rehabilitation

TOOTH WEAR AND FAILING DENTITION

CORE PRINCIPLE

The choice to restore follows disease control, available space and prognosis, not tooth-wear severity alone.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Palatal erosion and acid exposureIntrinsic/extrinsic erosive process Investigate and control cause before definitive veneers
Flat matching occlusal facets with parafunctionAttrition may coexist with erosion Record baseline BEWE/photographs and functional risk
No restorative space despite short crownsDentoalveolar compensation Consider additive Dahl approach when appropriate
Isolated cusp pain on release with crackPossible incomplete cracked toothProtect cusp, assess pulp and crack extent before crown

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

A Dahl approach uses relative axial tooth movement to create interocclusal space, but requires appropriate patient selection and consent about temporary disclusion and monitoring. Crown-lengthening or tooth reduction can be alternatives with different biological costs. An asymptomatic crack without pulpal complications should not automatically receive RCT.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A 40-year-old with compensated anterior wear and stable posterior support needs conservative additive planning rather than routine full-mouth preparation. Another patient with active vomiting-related erosion requires medical liaison and prevention first.

EXAM TRAP

The absence of space is not evidence that increasing the entire OVD is always indicated.

UNIT 11 Implant prosthodontics at Level 2 and digital workflow s

IN ONE MINUTE

Primary stability is mechanical, two implants are the m inim um for the edentulous mandible, and peri-im plantitis needs bone loss.

Distances: 1.5 mm to a tooth, 3 mm

between implants, 2 mm above the IAN .

Screw -retained crowns are retrievable; cem ent-retained crowns risk residual subgingival cement.

Guided surgery merges CBCT (D IC OM ) with surface scans (S TL).

A t Level 2 you are expected to provide and maintain simple im plant-retained prostheses (single tooth, simple overdenture) and

to diagnose peri-im plant disease; implant assessm ent, planning and placem ent are Level 3.

11.1 Implant fundam entals

O sseointegration (B rånem ark): direct structural and functional connection between living bone and the surface of a load- bearing implant, with no intervening soft tissue.

Stability: primary stability is mechanical (at placem ent); secondary stability is biological (bone rem odelling over w eeks). The "stability dip" occurs about 2–4 weeks after placem ent.

Spacing guidelines (approxim ate): 1.5 mm from implant to adjacent tooth; 3 mm between implants; at least 1.5–2 mm of buccal

bone; 2 mm safety margin above the inferior alveolar canal.

Loading protocols (ITI): immediate (w ithin 1 w eek), early (1 week to 2 m onths), conventional (after 2 m onths).

Connections: external hex (historic, more screw loosening), internal hex or octagon, conical (M orse taper) — better sealand stability. Platform switching (narrow er abutm ent than im plant) may reduce crestal bone loss.

Risk factors for failure and peri-im plantitis: smoking, poorly controlled diabetes, history of periodontitis, poor plaque control, lack of maintenance, radiotherapy to the site, high-dose IV antiresorptives, bruxism .

11.2 Implant prostheses

OP TIO N KEYPO IN TS

Tw o-im plant mandibular overdenture

M cG ill (2002) and York (2009) consensus m inim um standard for the edentulous mandible; big gains in satisfaction and function

Maxillary implant overdenture Usually 4 or more implants; palateless design possible

Single implant crown Screw -retained (retrievable, no subgingival cem ent) or cem ent-retained (passive, aesthetic access, but residual cement causes peri-im plant disease)

Fixed full-arch Level 3; passive fit essential; distal cantilevers kept short relative to implant spread

Most common complications: overdentures — loss of retention and attachm ent insert replacem ent, denture fracture opposite implants; single crowns — abutm ent screw loosening, ceram ic chipping; fixed full-arch — veneer chipping and fracture.

Implants have no periodontal ligam ent: no physiological m ovem ent or proprioception (osseoperception only). In a tooth– implant connected bridge the differential mobility causes problem s: avoid.

11.3 P eri-im plant health and disease (2017 World W orkshop)

COND ITIO N FIND IN G S MANAGEMENT LEVEL

P eri-im plant health

No erythem a, bleeding or suppuration; no bone loss beyond initial rem odelling

Maintenance

P eri-im plant m ucositis

Bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing; no bone loss beyond initial rem odelling; reversible

Level 2: mechanical debridem ent,

OH I, check prosthesis design, adjuncts

loss. Without baseline: bone level 3 mm or more apical to the implant

platform and P P D6 mm or more with bleeding

Level 3 (w henN H S responsibility)

Maintenance: patient-perform ed cleaning (interdental brushes, floss under bars), professional debridem ent with instrum ents

that do not scratch titanium , annual review .

11.4 Digital prosthodontics

Intraoral scanners: excellent for short spans and single units; accuracy (trueness and precision) falls over full arches due to stitching errors. Limitations: subgingival margins, blood and saliva, edentulous mucosa (cannot m ucodisplace or border m ould).

File formats: S TL (surface triangles, open format, no colour), PLY or O B J (can carry colour and texture), DIC OM (CBCT and

medical im aging). Merging DIC OM with S TL enables guided implant surgery.

S ubtractive manufacture (m illing): dense, homogeneous materials (pre-polym erised PMMA , zirconia, lithium disilicate, PEEK , Co-Cr, Ti); limited by bur size for fine detail.

Additive manufacture (3D printing): stereolithography (S LA ), digital light processing (D LP ), selective laser melting (m etals).

Uses: models, surgical guides, trays, splints, temporary crowns, printed denture bases and teeth.

Digital complete dentures: fewer visits, records stored for easy duplication, milled bases have low residual m onom er and excellent fit; limitations in recording functional borders and in complex jaw relations.

Digital smile design and virtual m ock-ups help communication and consent; a physical m ock-up from a w ax-up is still useful for patient approval.

Virtual articulators and facial scanning integrate facial references; jaw motion tracking can record dynam ic occlusion.

Examiner traps — Unit 11

The stability dip falls at 2–4 weeks, as primary gives way to secondary stability.

A void rigidly connecting a tooth to an implant.

Intraoral scans are least accurate on mobile edentulous mucosa and long spans.

Clean titanium with instrum ents that do not scratch it.

pages.title: S14 | Implants: planning, disease and maintenance
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 7 → Diploma Unit 11

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2a.19 · 2c.2, 2c.4–2c.5, 2c.21

CORE PRINCIPLE

The Diploma emphasis is prosthodontic choices, recognition of disease and safe referral—not advanced implant surgery.

01 Prosthesis-first assessment

Identify the missing-tooth problem, desired prosthesis, smile line, available restorative space, adjacent teeth, occlusion, cleansability and patient priorities before considering implant feasibility.

02 Restorative design choices

Discuss the implications of screw-retained versus cement-retained prostheses. Screw access and retrievability can be advantages; excess subgingival cement is a recognised peri-implant inflammatory risk.

03 Detect complications

Examine peri-implant tissues, bleeding or suppuration, plaque control, restoration integrity and radiographic bone levels in context. Distinguish peri-implant mucositis from suspected peri-implantitis, document findings and arrange appropriate review/referral.

04 Long-term maintenance

Outline hygiene, supportive care, prosthesis access and implant-specific complications such as screw loosening, chipping and biological inflammation. An implant surviving in situ is not synonymous with a successful functioning restoration.

05 Do not overextend the scope

Sinus grafting, ridge augmentation, complex surgical templates, advanced full-arch implants and specialist peri-implant surgery appear in F Pros but should not be treated as routine Level 2 Diploma procedures.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Source NHS complexity chart directs complex implant planning and multidisciplinary implant-related care to Level 3.

pages.title: S15 | Digital workflows: strengths and limitations
pages.html:
F Pros Chapter 13 → Diploma Unit 11

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 1.9 · 2c.5 · 3a.5

CORE PRINCIPLE

Digital is a method—not proof that the impression, plan or result is accurate.

01 When an intraoral scan helps

Good access and controlled moisture permit rapid review and rescanning, especially for single units and shorter spans. Accuracy depends on visibility, scanner technique, software and surface characteristics.

02 When conventional methods remain useful

Full-arch stitching, movable edentulous tissues, functional impressions, subgingival bleeding margins and multiple-implant passive fit can create limitations. Use a validated technique and verification where indicated.

03 Know the file vocabulary

Trueness means closeness to the reference; precision means repeatability. STL contains surface geometry; DICOM is used for volumetric imaging. Merging scans can support prosthetically led planning, but mismatches must be checked.

04 CAD/CAM options

Milling provides reproducible dense industrial materials but has tool-radius and material-waste limits. Printing is useful for models, trays and provisionals; post-curing and material indication affect outcomes.

05 Records and consent

Use digital design to explain options, not to promise a perfect smile. Save source files securely, document revisions, and check the limits and validation status of the individual device/workflow.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Complex guided implant surgery and advanced computer-assisted rehabilitation belong under appropriately trained services.

Source material: F Pros pp. 37–38 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 11: Peri-implant mucositis versus peri-implantitis
pages.html:
Peri-implant mucositis versus peri-implantitis

IMPLANTS AND DIGITAL WORKFLOWS

CORE PRINCIPLE

Bleeding and suppuration alone are not enough to diagnose progressive peri-implant bone loss; use probing, baseline radiographs and the course of the disease.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Bleeding on gentle probing; no progressive bone lossPeri-implant mucositis Biofilm control, prosthesis cleansability and re-evaluation
Inflammation plus progressive crestal bone lossPeri-implantitis more likely Determine treatability, disease severity and referral need
Deep sulcus after implantation without reference baselineDifficult to diagnose by probing depth aloneSeek prior records and assess serial imaging/clinical changes
Loose implant crown; normal peri-implant tissuesPossible prosthetic screw complicationDifferentiate component looseness from loss of osseointegration

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The EFP S3 pathway supports supportive peri-implant care and non-surgical biofilm removal for mucositis, with assessment of prosthesis access and risk factors. For peri-implantitis, start with diagnosis and non-surgical treatment, re-evaluate and involve a suitably competent practitioner for advanced treatment where necessary.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A bleeding site around an implant with stable radiographic bone and inadequate floss access is not managed like one with suppuration and increasing radiographic bone loss. In the first, focus on plaque control and cleansability; in the second, investigate disease progression and treatment complexity.

EXAM TRAP

Microbial communities are polymicrobial; no single "peri-implantitis pathogen" explains all presentations.

pages.title: Edition 2 | Unit 11: The mandibular two-implant overdenture: space and attachments
pages.html:
The mandibular two-implant overdenture: space and attachments

IMPLANTS AND DIGITAL WORKFLOWS

CORE PRINCIPLE

The McGill two-implant mandibular overdenture is an important evidence-based option, but attachment choice follows interarch space, implant position, dexterity and maintenance.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Two parallel interforaminal implants; adequate spaceStud/Locator-type retention may be suitableAssess wear inserts, hygiene, implant divergence and replacement
Two implants with divergence or splinting needBar-clip system may be consideredRequires greater vertical restorative space and access
Limited restorative height under proposed dentureInsufficient space for matrix, acrylic and teethMeasure and redesign before selecting an attachment
Opposing maxillary complete dentureUpper denture stability, wear and load matterConsider occlusion and maxillary support before increasing retention

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Published restorative-space figures vary with attachment family and denture design; they are not universal: verify manufacturer minimum stack height, denture base thickness, teeth clearance, hygiene and repair access. Low-profile studs generally demand less space than many bar assemblies. Implant location and lingual inclination influence the path of insertion and attachment wear.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A severely resorbed mandible has enough room for a low-profile attachment but not a proposed bar with clips, acrylic and teeth. A stud may be the better restoration provided implant alignment, support and maintenance are satisfactory.

EXAM TRAP

"Two implants" is not a mandate for every patient; patient factors, access, cost and anatomy govern consent and selection.

12.2 Removable partial dentures

PROBLEM LIKELY CAUSES

Fram ew ork does not seat at fit

Distorted impression or cast, tray m ovem ent, rest seats not recorded, investm ent or casting error, soft tissue im pingem ent — check with disclosing medium ; if gross, re-im pression and remake

Clasp loose / lost retention Clasp distorted (patient removing by the clasp), work hardening, wrong undercut, wear

Clasp fracture Fatigue at the shoulder, repeated adjustm ent of Co-Cr (low ductility), porosity in casting

A butm ent pain or mobility Occlusal overload, rest not seated, free-end saddle rotation (needs reline), clasp active at rest

Free-end saddle sinks and indirect retainer lifts

Ridge resorption — reline the saddle

Gingival inflam mation under the denture

Gingival coverage, plaque, inadequate relief, poor hygiene

C aries of abutm ents Plaque retention at clasps and minor connectors, high sugar intake

Food under saddles U nder-extension, poor saddle fit

12.3 Complete dentures — maintenance

Recall: at least annually for mucosal examination, fit and occlusal wear.

R eline or rebase when fit is lost but the polished and occlusal surfaces are acceptable; remake when O V D , aesthetics, or occlusion are also wrong.

Repairs: fracture lines must be reassem bled accurately before a cast is poured; self-cured acrylic repairs are weaker; investigate the cause of repeated fractures ( Section 7.9 ).

Denture hygiene: brush with a soft brush and soap or non-abrasive cleanser over a basin of water, soak overnight (hypochlorite only for acrylic, nom etal), leave out at night.

12.4 Laboratory and external factors

Errors arise at: impressions (distortion, drag, voids), casts (air bubbles, abraded dies), articulation (incorrect records), wax and investm ent (distortion), casting (porosity, incom plete casting), processing (acrylic porosity, raised O V D from flash), and finishing (over-polished fitting surfaces).

Prevention: clear written prescriptions, quality control at each clinical stage (inspect impressions and casts on return), good communication including photographs and shade, agreed delivery times.

12.5 Assessing outcom es

Compare outcom es with published survival data and with the patient's goals (patient-reported outcom es: comfort, function, aesthetics, satisfaction).

Survival = the prosthesis is still in situ; success = in situ and free of complications. Ask which is reported when interpreting studies.

pages.title: S16 | Failure analysis and measurable success
pages.html:
F Pros Chapters 5–7 and 11 → Diploma Unit 12

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2c.21–2c.27 · 3a.2–3a.8

CORE PRINCIPLE

A sound answer diagnoses why a prosthesis failed before choosing the repair or remake.

01 Diagnose by category

Biological: new caries, pulpal symptoms, periodontal/peri-implant inflammation. Mechanical: fractured tooth/restoration, clasp failure, screw loosening or debond. Functional: occlusal interference, instability or inadequate support.

02 Review the sequence of failure

Ask when symptoms began, whether fit/occlusion altered, whether maintenance occurred and whether risk factors changed. Use history, clinical examination, photographs, tests, radiographs and old records as justified.

03 Correct cause—not appearance

An RPD repeatedly fracturing may reflect inadequate thickness, support or occlusal forces. A debonding crown may signal poor retention form. Excess cement, inaccessible hygiene and design can underlie peri-implant inflammation.

04 Audit outcomes

Document comfort, function, aesthetics, cleaning, biological health, mechanical integrity and patient satisfaction. Survival percentages alone do not capture complications or burden of maintenance.

05 Feedback to the plan

Treat failure as an opportunity to change the design, risk control, consent or review interval. Escalate repeated complex failures or combined specialist problems beyond Level 2 competence.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Case-based reasoning and honest complication communication are more important than memorising unsupported survival figures.

Source material: F Pros pp. 20, 22–26, 33–34 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

Failure analysis: diagnose before remake

COMPLICATIONS AND MAINTENANCE

CORE PRINCIPLE

A repeat complication is a test of the original design hypothesis. Recreating the same prosthesis without identifying the cause is rarely sound management.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Crown repeatedly decements Lack of resistance, short axial walls or occlusal overloadAssess prep geometry, fit, caries and path of insertion

A repair without patient-centred discussion of recurrence risk and follow-up is an incomplete treatment plan.

UNIT 13 Maintaining good practice: governance, law and communication

IN ONE MINUTE

M ontgom ery for consent, the MC A for capacity, candour when things gow rong, and adult records kept 11 years.

G DC : nine principles; enhanced C P D

100 hours in 5 years.

IR (M E )R duty holders and H TM 01-05 decontam ination.

Safeguarding: record and refer; never investigate yourself.

These are the most learnable marks in the paper: the answers follow UK law and G DC standards, not opinion. The rules below are for England unless stated; check devolved-nation equivalents.

13.1 Consent and capacity

Valid consent is inform ed, voluntary, given by a person with capacity, and specific to the treatm ent; it is a process,

docum ented in the notes, and can be withdraw nat anytime.

M ontgom ery v Lanarkshire (2015): the clinician must disclose material risks — those a reasonable person in the patient's position would consider significant, or that this particular patient would — and reasonable alternatives (including no treatm ent).

It replaced Bolam as the test for disclosure.

Bolam (1957): standard of care is that of a responsible body of professional opinion; Bolitho (1997): that opinion must withstand logical analysis. Both still apply to diagnosis and treatm ent (not disclosure).

Negligence requires duty of care, breach of that duty, causation, and resulting harm . Vicarious liability: an employer is liable for the acts of employees in the course of em ploym ent.

Mental Capacity A ct 2005 (E ngland and W ales) principles: presum e capacity; take all practicable steps to help the person decide; an unwise decision does not mean incapacity; actin best interests; choose the least restrictive option. Tw o-stage test: im pairm ent of mind or brain, then can the person understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate the decision? Capacity is decision-specific and tim e-specific.

Scotland: Adults with Incapacity (S cotland) A ct 2000.

Young people: 16–17-year-olds are presum ed to have capacity to consent (Fam ily Law Reform A ct 1969); under 16s may consent if Gillick competent.

Shared decision-m aking (N ICE NG 197): discuss benefits, risks, alternatives and doing nothing (BRAN ); use decision aids; check understanding.

13.2 GDCS tandards for the Dental Team — nine principles

Put patients' interests first.

Comm unicate effectively with patients.

Obtain valid consent.

Maintain and protect patients' inform ation.

Have a clear and effective complaints procedure.

Work with colleagues in a way that is in patients' best interests.

Maintain, develop and work within your professional knowledge and skills.

Raise concerns if patients are at risk.

Enhanced C P D (dentists): at least 100 verifiable hours per 5-year cycle, at least 10 hours in every 2-year period, with a personal developm ent plan; recom mended topics include medical emergencies, decontam ination, radiography and radiation protection, legal and ethical issues, complaints handling, oral cancer detection, safeguarding.

Appropriate indem nity is mandatory.

13.3 Duty of candour, incidents and complaints

Professional duty of candour (all registrants): be open and honest when something goes wrong, apologise, offer an appropriate remedy, explain the short- and long-term effects. Statutory duty of candour applies to C Q C -registered providers for notifiable safety incidents. A n apology is not an admission of liability.

Incident reporting: significant event analysis and root cause analysis locally; N H S patient safety events to the national system

(Learn from Patient Safety E vents); adverse drug reactions via MHRAY ellow Card; medical device incidents to MHRA ; serious

workplace injuries and dangerous occurrences under RID DO R to the H SE .

Never events are wholly preventable serious incidents (e.g., w rong-site surgery including wrong tooth extraction).

N H S complaints (E ngland): acknow ledge within 3 working days; resolve locally; complaint normally made within 12 months of

the event or of becom ing aware; escalation to the P arliam entary and Health Service Om budsm an. Private patients: the Dental

Complaints Service. Respond in writing, apologise where appropriate, explain, and describe actions taken.

Raising concerns (w histleblow ing) is protected by the Public Interest Disclosure A ct 1998; G DC requires registrants to raise

concerns even if they are not the employer.

13.4 Records and inform ation governance

Records must be accurate, contem poraneous, legible, attributable, and never altered without a dated, signed note of the change.

Retention (NHSE ngland guidance): adults at least 11 years after the last treatm ent; children until age 25 or 11 years after the

last treatm ent, whichever is longer. R adiographs and models are part of the record.

UKGDPR and the Data Protection A ct 2018: lawful basis for processing, security, data m inim isation. Subject access requests answered within one month, normally free of charge. C aldicott principles govern confidential inform ation sharing.

Confidentiality may be breached with consent, when required by law (court order), or in the public interest (serious harm to others) — share the m inim um necessary.

13.5 Radiation protection

IR R 17 (Ionising R adiations Regulations 2017): protect workers and public; employer registers with the H SE , appoints a

radiation protection adviser (R PA ) and radiation protection supervisor (R P S ), sets local rules and a controlled area (for intraoral sets, typically within 1.5 mof the tube and patient and within the primary beam until attenuated).

IR (M E )R 2017: protect patients; duty holders are employer, referrer, practitioner (justifies) and operator; justification,

optim isation (A LAR P ), clinical evaluation and recording of every exposure; pregnancy enquiries where relevant.

O ptim isation tools: rectangular collim ation, film holders, fastest image receptor, appropriate kV and exposure, quality

assurance program me and audit of image quality.

13.6 Infection prevention and control (H TM 01-05)

D econtam ination cycle

Transport → Cleaning → Inspection → S terilisation → Storage → Use

Cleaning: w asher-disinfector is best practice; ultrasonic or manual acceptable for essential quality. Inspection under illum inated magnification.

Steam sterilisation at 134–137°C for at least 3 minutes. Vacuum (type B ) sterilisers are needed for wrapped and hollow or lum ened instrum ents; non-vacuum (type N ) for unwrapped solid instrum ents.

P rosthodontic items: rinse and disinfect impressions, records, try-ins and appliances before they goto or comeback from the laboratory; label as disinfected.

13.7 Safeguarding, equality and diversity

Safeguarding children and adults at risk: recognise (injuries to head, face and mouth; dental neglect; unusual behaviour), record, refer (practice safeguarding lead, local authority children's or adult social care; police if immediate danger). Do not investigate yourself; inform ation sharing to protect a child or adult is lawful.

Female genital mutilation: regulated health professionals in England and Wales must report known cases in under-18s to the police.

Equality A ct 2010: nine protected characteristics (age, disability, gender reassignm ent, marriage and civil partnership,

pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation); duty to make reasonable adjustm ents (e.g., wheelchair access, longer appointm ents, easy-read inform ation).

13.8 Clinical governance, audit and evidence

Pillars: clinical effectiveness and audit, risk m anagem ent, education and training, patient and public involvem ent, inform ation

m anagem ent, staff m anagem ent, research.

Audit cycle

Choose topic → Set standard → Measure current practice → Compare with standard → Im plem ent change →

R e-audit (closes the loop)

Audit measures practice against a standard; research generates new knowledge; service evaluation describes current service without a standard.

Quality im provem ent: P lan–D o–S tudy–A ct cycles, run charts, root cause analysis, significant event analysis, human factors, checklists (e.g., local safety standards for invasive procedures).

Hierarchy of evidence: system atic review and m eta-analysis of R C Ts → R CT → cohort → case–control → case series and reports → expert opinion. GRADE rates certainty of evidence.

Key statistics: sensitivity (true positive rate) and specificity (true negative rate); positive predictive value depends on prevalence; number needed to treat = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction; a 95% confidence interval crossing 1 (for ratios) or 0 (for differences) is not statistically significant.

Ireland). Professional regulator: G DC .

Level 2 decisions, consent and escalation

GOVERNANCE AND COMMUNICATION

CORE PRINCIPLE

The Diploma tests the independent judgement of an enhanced-skills practitioner, not specialist surgery. Defensible care includes knowing when to refer.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Stable, maintainable prosthesis with local defectA repair or review may have best risk-benefit ratioDiscuss conservative alternatives and monitor
Uncontrolled disease before extensive restorationDefinitive prosthesis is premature Stabilise caries, periodontitis and risk factors first
Complex rehabilitation, advanced perio/implant surgeryOutcome beyond operator competenceRefer with diagnostic records and clear clinical question
Persistent ulcer, progressive neuropathy or airway threatTime-critical red flag Urgent escalation rather than repeated denture adjustment

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Consent requires an individualised explanation of likely benefit, risks, uncertainty, maintenance, complications, alternatives and the option of no replacement. Record decision capacity, patient priorities and how risks were communicated. Relevant audit outcomes include prosthesis survival, patient-reported function, recalls, repair incidence and clinical stability.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A patient asks for multiple implants despite active Stage IV periodontitis and poor attendance. A specialist referral and disease-control sequence is more defensible than immediate implant surgery even if the procedure is technically possible.

EXAM TRAP

Passing an examination does not replace local credentialing or establish competence to undertake every Level 2 procedure.

pages.title: S17 | Final-week integrated decision traps
pages.html:
F Pros crash notebook → Diploma Unit 14

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES Across 1, 2a, 2b, 2c and 3a–3b

CORE PRINCIPLE

Use these prompts to test the decisions common to both source notebooks—not as official examination predictions.

01 Diagnose before intervening

A suspicious lesion needs investigation/referral, not camouflage by a prosthesis. In ambiguous test results, repeat or complement the clinical examination instead of forcing a diagnosis.

02 Stabilise and preserve

Caries/periodontal control precedes complex definitive work. Prefer additive or reversible approaches where they meet the need; no treatment is a legitimate comparator for a missing tooth.

03 Design with forces in mind

RPD support precedes clasp selection; a distal extension needs indirect retention and maintenance. Low denture retention can be functional-border failure rather than an adhesive deficiency.

04 Material chemistry matters

A post retains, not reinforces. Silane is for suitable silica-based surfaces, not zirconia. Good cement cannot rescue a short and severely over-tapered preparation.

05 Recognise your level

Routine Level 2 planning may include moderately difficult tooth replacement; complex multidisciplinary care, severe parafunction, full-mouth reorganisation, complex implants and specialist trauma management need escalation.

06 Answer the clinical question asked

Look for “first,” “most appropriate” or “least invasive,” and select the patient-safe next action rather than the most sophisticated possible procedure.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Revision prompts are educational summaries of the supplied notes; exact standards and medications require current verification.

Source material: F Pros pp. 5–7, 10, 12, 15, 17, 20, 23, 26, 28, 30, 32, 34, 36, 38 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

pages.html:
Numbers are conditional: SBA crosswalk and evidence

HIGH-YIELD REVISION

CORE PRINCIPLE

Treat measurement values as decision aids. Always ask what material, patient, laboratory system and measurement method produced the number.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75 mm survey gaugesMeasure retentive undercuts, not automatic clasp prescriptionsCross-check material modulus, geometry, abutment and path
2-4 mm freeway space; varying individual valuesA jaw relation cross-check, not a fixed endpointCorrelate speech, facial support, comfort and repeatability
Crown/ceramic reduction valuesDepend on material and manufacturerCheck required bulk, ferrule and resistance form
Implant attachment vertical heightDepends on components plus denture thicknessMeasure available interarch distance before selecting system

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The updated Volume II SBA bank is 1,500 questions: 270 Foundation, 730 Intermediate and 500 Advanced. Filter by Block A for applied anatomy, B pathology, C materials, D medical, E assessment, F RPD, G complete dentures, H fixed, I occlusion, J failing dentition, K implants, L maintenance, M governance; Block N is integrated cases. Advanced questions are dispersed across their clinical blocks, so the original source's Q1001-Q2000 block numbering is obsolete.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

In an SBA, a numerical choice is strong only when the stem supplies the missing constraints. A 0.5-mm undercut plus a short Co-Cr clasp cannot be answered by a memorised "gold clasp" association without checking geometry.
